audits.title: Border inspection posts

recommendations.text: The major deficiencies related to the procedures (identification and selection, procedure, and transit/warehouse/ship supplier procedures) should be corrected immediately and in particular: 16/11/00 - 64318 29 § Denmark should ensure that the staff in the BIPs improve their systems for obtaining information on incoming and outgoing consignments and take an active part in order to guarantee that all consignments related to veterinary checks from third countries arriving in the BIPs are under the supervision of the official veterinarians and are checked in accordance with the import requirements to this. In particular it should be focused on the checks (documentary checks) carried out in the BIPs and the supervision of the warehouses and ship supplier allowed to store non-EC-conforming consignments. § The immediate suspension of imports from non-approved vessels or establishments and imports without valid health certification should be ensured. § The immediate suspension of imports of consignments through BIPs which are not approved for those categories should be ensured. § The immediate suspension of unloading of frozen fish in Skagen should be ensured.

Action should be taken to correct all other deficiencies noted in § this report (general findings, veterinary staff, facilities, equipment, hygiene, documentation, registration, identification and selection, procedure, kitchen waste and transit/warehouse procedures, fees, Intra-Community checks). In any event all deficiencies should be corrected within three months of receipt of the translated final report and in particular: BIP staff: Shortage of staff in all BIPs (except Neksø), in particular in Aalborg, Hirtshals and Fredericia and adequate training in especially in relation to procedures and systems for identification and selection of consignments. § Facilities: The deficiencies related to the construction of the facilities in Aarhus (live animals), København port (live animals), Køge (products) and Kolding-Billund airport (products) should be corrected.

The deficiencies of the facilities (construction other than those in 8.1.2) referred to in this report should be corrected within six months of receipt of the translated final report and in particular for: § Aalborg, Hirtshals, Aarhus, Hanstholm, København airport, Neksø, Fredericia, Esbjerg: the facilities for products; 16/11/00 - 64318 30 § Hirtshals, Kolding-Billund airport and port: the facilities for live animals. 8.2. To the Commission It is recommended that the Commission Services: 8.2.1. Consider the withdrawal of the approval of the border inspection posts mentioned under 8.1.2. and 8.1.3. if satisfactory guarantees in relation to the approval (type of category) are not provided within the relevant time limit by the Danish Authority and/or if the time limits are not met. 8.2.2. Consider to change the name of the BIP of Kolding-Billund port to Kolding port and of Kolding-Billund airport to Billund airport in the list of approved border inspection posts. 8.2.3. Consider the limitation of the approval for København airport, Kolding-Billund airport, Fredericia, and Køge to packed products only.

Consider assessing the Danish transposition of Council Directive 85/73/EEC, as amended and consolidated by Council Directive 96/43/EC, to determine whether, in relation to the charging of fees in BIPs, it is in line with EC-legislation.
Consider assessing the Danish transposition of Council Directive 97/78/EC and Commission Decisions 97/794/EC and 2000/25/EC to determine whether it is in line with EC-legislation.
Consider reviewing of the model of the Annex B laid down in Commission Decision 93/13/EEC with regard to the requirements laid down in Articles 5 and 11 of Council Directive 97/78/EC.

Consider a follow up mission to approved free and customs warehouses and to authorised ship suppliers.¦ 16/11/00 - 64318 31 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/1031/2000. audits.title: Potato sector

recommendations.text: Prohibit the production of seed potatoes on a farm in the year after a ring rot infestation is found as required by Annex IV, point 4.1(b) of Council Directive 93/85/EEC.
Request the use of certified seed in ware potato production for three years following the infestation year as required by Annex IV, point 4.1 of Council Directive 93/85/EEC.

Conduct PCN pathotype testing when farmers intend to use PCN resistant varieties on PCN infested plots where the pathotypes are not known in order to fulfil the requirements of Article 8, point 1(b) of Council Directive 69/465/EEC. In addition, it is advised to the competent authorities in Denmark to:
Increase the sampling and laboratory testing for brown rot in the ware potato production.

Test waste water from washing potatoes at starch factories for R. solanacearum (and possibly also for C.m.s.) and potatoes on farms used for its disposal for both C.m.s. and R. solanacearum. Denmark is requested to report to the Commission by 31 May 2001 on action taken on the above points. 10.2. Recommendations to the Commission Services It is recommended to the Commission Services to initiate a review and possible modification of the requirements in the ring rot directive, 93/85/EEC (Annex IV, point 4.1) for use of certified seed on infected farms. 24 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/1119/2000 Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report The Danish plant protection authority (PD) welcomes the report and undertakes to fully implement the recommendations and advisory points. 25

audits.title: BSE

recommendations.text: The Competent Authority should consider adopting a second level of controls to ensure and demonstrate that: · All eligible animals are being sampled; and · All samples end up in the laboratory and are examined.

The competent Authority should consider giving instructions for the controls to be carried out in slaughterhouses and a system to record these controls. These instructions and records should provide additional documentary evidence to demonstrate that sampling at slaughterhouse level is in compliance with the requirements. 9.2. Total Feed-ban (1) The Competent Authority should consider a more targeted approach to the sampling program. Sampling should be targeted at materials, times and places, where the probability of finding forbidden substances (MBM and unlicensed fishmeal) is highest. (2) The Competent Authority should ensure that the sampling techniques as laid down in Commission Directive 76/371/EEC and the corresponding Danish instructions are fully understood and complied with.
The Competent Authority should pay particular attention to controls on transport and cleansing of transport vehicles.

The Competent Authority should ensure that fishmeal is not delivered directly to holdings where ruminants are being kept. Direct deliveries of fishmeal from feed-mills (and fishmeal plants, as 30 appropriate) to farms should be under the control of the Competent Authority. 9.3. Specified Risk Materials (1) The Central Competent Authority should consider issue instructions on the practical implementation of controls along the SRM chain and establish a system of recording control activities. (2) The Central Competent Authority should take action to ensure that all SRM is stained efficiently. (3) The Central Competent Authority should ensure that reconciliation of SRM at the various stages is done in such a way, that collection and disposal of all SRM can be demonstrated. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT 3282/2001 Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report The Danish authorities announced in their written comments of 5 October 2001 that they have taken the following actions in relation to the recommendations: · A database is being established to ensure that all eligible animals are being sampled, all samples end up in the laboratory and are examined for BSE. In the slaughterhouses there will be a possibility to verify the identity of animals i.e. the breed, sex, age and colour of each animal. · More precise instructions and checklists will be elaborated in order to demonstrate the controls carried out by the competent authority in slaughterhouses. · As regards the targeting of feed-controls, instructions for the inspectors are being prepared. The annual control plan for next year is being revised and will apply a more targeted approach. · The competent authority will pay particular attention to controls on transport of feeding-stuff and cleansing of vehicles. The inspectors have been instructed to do so in meetings of 12 March and 22 May 2001. Additional written instructions were given in June 2001. Hauliers and feed mills will be informed about the rules on transportation. · A system will be established to control documentation in slaughterhouses, cutting plants, butcher's shops and the SRM plant in order to crosscheck the consignments sent and received. · The staining of SRM will be enforced and methods for the demonstration of stain in MBM will be established in the official laboratories. · Reconciliation of SRM between slaughterhouses and the SRM plant will be enforced. 31

audits.title: Fishery products and live Bivalve Molluscs

recommendations.text: Legislation The Danish Environmental Protection Agency has been asked for a statement regarding the implementation of Council Directive 79/923/EEC. The Agency has referred to reports from 1996 and 1999 performed by the Ministry of Environment and Energy describing the implementation of all environmental directives regarding waters. Both reports are sent officially to the Commission. When the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration (DVFA) receives more detailed information this will be forwarded to the Commission services.

Laboratories Procedures for approval and supervision of laboratories are in process. Where appropriate the laboratories have to be accredited. DVFA (Mørkhøj) will take the necessary actions regarding reviewing the performance of the bioassay including sampling and analysis. Where necessary the performance procedure will be rectified to make sure that the methods are performed correctly and according to the official method. In September 2001 the laboratory performing the bioassay has received an accreditation on the method.

Official controls Actions have been taken to strengthen the official controls. The regional system has been re-evaluated. The budget for 2002 has been allocated resources equivalent to 19 persons intended for official control in relation to the implementation of own-check procedures including HACCP in the establishments. This financial resource is planned to continue until 2005. Furthermore, specified results and report systems are incorporated in the employment contracts for the Regional Directors from 2002.

Monitoring programme on bivalve molluscs DVFA (Mørkhøj) is at present working with different ideas on how to verify and confirm the reliability of the procedures and results from the sampling performed by the fishermen. This supervision will eventually include random sampling. DVFA (Mørkhøj) is planning to approve the laboratories involved in the monitoring programme on bivalve molluscs. This approval will include check of the laboratories to see whether they fulfil their obligations in relation to the bivalve molluscs monitoring programme.

Sites visited The Regional Offices (RO) have made follow-up reactions regarding deficiencies in the visited plants. Problems of a more general scope are discussed at meetings for inspectors from all Regional Offices. Furthermore, the Directorate of Fisheries (DF) and DVFA (Mørkhøj) are drawing up instructions concerning hygiene checks in auction halls and for the landing of molluscs. 24

audits.title: Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSE)

recommendations.text: To implement without delay compulsory notification of all TSEs in animals. 27
To increase efforts already made to establish a second level of control in order to ensure and to demonstrate that all eligible bovine animals are sampled and that all samples are examined.

To ensure that there is documentary evidence from official controls at slaughterhouse level that sampling is in compliance with the requirements. With regard to TSE controls in ovine and caprine animals (EC Reg. 999/2001):

To issue clear guidelines for the official controls on identification and registration in small ruminants and a system to record these controls and their results in order to demonstrate that the relevant requirements are enforced.
To evaluate the sampling programme periodically in order to ensure that over- or under-representation, for example of any breed or production type of animals, does not occur.
To establish a training programme in order to increase the level of awareness among the practitioners, breeders, keepers and handlers of small ruminants with respect to TSEs in these species.
To establish as soon as possible the contingency plan for TSEs in small ruminants. With regard to the feed ban:

To consider increasing the proportion of targeted samples for detection of Meat and Bone Meal (or unlicensed fishmeal) within the monitoring programme. The presentation of results should be divided between samples taken as a screening of the various feed stuffs and samples targeted at areas where it is most likely to detect a violation of the feed ban.
To consider including farmer's own transports in the controls for possible cross- contamination.
To apply the authorisation requirements of Annex I, point 6 of Commission Decision 2001/9/EC on home compounders using fishmeal.

To ensure that farms with both ruminant and monogastric species using feeds containing fishmeal are controlled before they can avail of the derogation foreseen in Commission Decision 2001/9/EC, Annex I, pt. 9. With regard to SRM:

To consider developing more detailed instructions on official controls including forms for record keeping and/or implement a system of audits from the central level in order to ensure a sufficient level of control in the various regions.

To ensure that the companies' own checks programmes include elements of checks/controls (including records from these) in order to make it possible for the official services to verify the efficacy of these programmes.
To ensure that staining of Specified Risk Material is carried out effectively. 28

To include the SRM rendering plant in the official controls regarding channelling/reconciliation of SRM in order to verify that all plants producing SRM are delivering reasonable amounts to this rendering plant. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/8572/2002 The Danish competent authorities informed the FVO in their response to the draft report on actions already taken or planned to be taken: With regard to epidemio-surveillance 1) That the Infectious Diseases Act will be amended so that in addition to BSE and Scrapie all other TSEs in animals will be included in the list over notifiable diseases. This is expected to be completed within two months. 2) That in order to ensure and demonstrate that all eligible bovines are sampled, random tests will be carried out by using a specific search tool, combining the bovine database with the TSE database, this will hopefully start in the later part of the year. This review is expected to take place in October 2002. Furthermore, the two regions where establishments were inspected have been asked to take immediate steps to rectify any shortcomings and all regions have received a written request to check whether the same deficiencies exist in other slaughterhouses. With regard to TSE controls in ovine and caprine animals 4) That a new system for ID and registration in small ruminants is in the process of being adopted. The programme is expected to enter into force on 1 October 2002. The programme includes: ear tagging with two tags within 20 days, movement registration in a database, herd lists including each individual animal, movement documents and monitoring of the system by the Plant Directorate (visits in around 5% of the herds each year). 5) That an evaluation of the sampling programme for small ruminants will be carried out in order to make sampling more representative. However, breed and production type can not currently be taken into account in the 29 monitoring programme since there are no records in the DVFA concerning this. The age is however checked by dentition. 6) That all registered sheep and goat breeders have received a publication describing the clinical signs. An information campaign is also considered for people who handle small ruminants on a daily basis (2003). The RVFCAs will also arrange courses for their staff. 7) That a contingency plan for TSEs in small ruminants is under development and will be finalised within the next six months. There are however already measures in place regarding what action would be taken in the event of TSE in small ruminants. Furthermore, measures in respect of movement of potentially contaminated feedingstuffs etc. will be included in the next revision of the Order on the surveillance of TSE in sheep and goats. With regard to the feed ban 8) That the majority of the samples taken in 2002 will be targeted and the results will be presented in a way that distinguishes between random sampling and targeted sampling. 9) That revised control instructions for feed stuff controls on farms are being prepared and these will address the issue of cleaning of transport vehicles. These instructions are expected to be implemented on 1 October 2002. With regard to SRM 12) That in respect of official controls on the SRM chain a new circular is being drawn up concerning detailed checks by the RVFCAs on the handling of SRM including checklists and record requirements. A copy of the draft has been provided to the FVO. That the DVFA's results-based contract contains a performance target whereby the DVFA must carry out inspections in all RVFCAs in 2002. These inspections will look at a number of fundamental aspects of these authorities` activities. These inspections are not intended to actually review the RVFCAs checks in certain areas of the legislation, they are more of a tool for the DVFA and RVFCAs to carry out uniform checks nation wide. A report will be prepared for each inspection as well as a general report for all the inspections. 13) That the variation in quality of own-checks will be addressed by a new guideline on handling specified risk material. This document of which a copy has been provided to the FVO, provides the legal requirements as well as guidelines on the practical implementation. Furthermore, it also gives details on the most necessary components in the own-checks programme and checklists that can be used. 14) That the recommendation on staining will be addressed in the new circular to the RVFCA concerning checks on the handling of SRM, and furthermore, the companies will be notified about the requirements. 30 15) That the inclusion of the SRM rendering plant in the channelling/reconciliation of SRM will be addressed through the revised guideline and the revised circular. 31

audits.title: Newcastle disease

recommendations.text: The CA should put further emphasis on the epidemiological inquiries and endeavour that all relevant epidemiological information is available to both local and national units involved. 9

Denmark should endeavour to improve the effectiveness and speed of communication with the relevant competent authorities in neighbouring countries in which restrictive measures for the poultry industry should apply.

Denmark should endeavour to improve the effectiveness and speed of communication with the relevant competent authorities in Member States or third countries, which received export consignments of poultry or potentially infected poultry products.

The control measures in the different protection and surveillance zones should be reinforced. For this purpose, further improvements are necessary to indicate more clearly the borders of the different zones to the public. The veterinary authorities should reinforce their collaboration with enforcement authorities such as the police in order to increase the level and quality of policing.

In addition to point (4), the CA should ensure that poultry meat does not receive the health mark foreseen in Article 3, (1) A (e) of Council Directive 71/118/EEC when not all provisions of Commission Decision 95/117/EC are correctly implemented. 8. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG (SANCO)8722/2002 Competent Authority's response to the recommendations in the report The CAs stated in their letter of 12 November 2002 (Ref. STM/BH File: 2002-20- 221-00326) that the ND outbreaks in Denmark apparently have been eradicated successfully. The latest outbreak was confirmed on 28 august 2002. Until 8 November 2002, 135 outbreaks have been confirmed (in 9 commercial farms and in 126 backyard holdings). Furthermore they added, in the same letter: "The Danish Veterinary and Food Administration was completely restructured in the year 2000 including reallocation of authority among Regional Veterinary and Food Authorities (RVFA). As a result of this, some inadequacies in procedures for a direct flow of information between RVFAs in outbreak situations were detected and corrected." In addition, they acknowledged recommendation 7.2 (5) and undertook corrective actions or improvements in relation to the other recommendations: ­ With regard to recommendation 7.2. (1), they indicated to further emphasise thorough epidemiological inquiries and corrective action being taken regarding the information from these inquiries being available and accessible to the relevant units. ­ With regard to recommendation 7.2. (2), they stated to have improved contacts from their central level with the corresponding authorities in the neighbouring country. ­ With regard to recommendation 7.2. (3), they indicated corrective action already taken in the field of communication of possibly infected consignments through 10 the ANIMO system. This aspect would also be dealt with in a revision of the Danish contingency plan for ND in 2003. ­ With regard to recommendation 7.2. (4), they noted that the issue of sign-posting will be re-evaluated in a revision of the Danish contingency plan for ND in 2003 and that the collaboration with enforcing authorities such as the police will be enhanced by meetings between authorities locally and centrally.

audits.title: Disease contingency plans

recommendations.text: To consider introducing a computer-based system for managing data on disease control tasks during outbreaks of major epizootic (OIE list A) diseases.
To ensure that sufficient rendering capacity can be rapidly made available in the case of an outbreak of epizootic disease.

To ensure that under the terms of the agreement currently being drawn up, the NRL can continue to provide sufficient diagnostic capacity to respond to outbreaks and expertise to support `peacetime' contingency planning activities.

To continue to work towards accreditation of the national reference laboratory to a recognised international standard, including developing procedures for the laboratory response to outbreaks of epizootic diseases.
To consider developing procedures for emergency vaccination.
To carry out practical simulation exercises, based on a scenario of disease outbreaks within Denmark, involving all services that would be involved in the event of an outbreak.
To consider further measures to encourage the reporting of cases of suspicion of epizootic disease.

To continue reviewing the disease contingency plans foreseen in EU legislation in the light of the findings of this mission. The Danish authorities should submit an action plan indicating the actions taken and planned in response to the conclusions and recommendations of this report, including a timetable for completion of these actions, within two months of receipt of the final, translated report. 10. audits.title: Control systems for the placing on the market and use of plant protection products and for residues in foodstuffs of plant origin

recommendations.text: The competent authority should increase the number of inspections and develop controls on the authorised use of plant protection products for controlling the marketing of plant protection products, in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC.

The competent authorities should establish co-ordinated procedures between the organisations involved in controls for uses of plant protection products, in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC.

The competent authorities should take all necessary steps to reduce the time-lapse between sampling and analysis for pesticide residues and ensure that enforcement and follow-up actions are taken in a systematic way without delay.
The competent authorities should ensure that sampling is carried out in accordance with Commission Directive 2002/63/EC.

In cases of MRL infringements, the competent authorities should consider to take into account the draft "Proposal on how to notify pesticide residues in foodstuffs in the Rapid Alert System for Foodstuffs" (SANCO/3346/2001). An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. ADDENDUM In their response to the draft report, the Danish authorities submitted a preliminary action plan. With regard to recommendation (1) and (2), the competent authorities stated that there are plans to improve co-ordination of controls on the uses of plant protection products. In relation to recommendation (3), the DVFA will start efforts to shorten the time-lap between sampling and analysis, and will take actions to ensure that the local control authorities are aware of the importance of follow-up actions. In relation to recommendation (4), DVFA holds seminars and will work out guidelines which will describe the sampling procedure in detail. recommendations.text: In relation to recommendation 1, the VFA issued Order No 7 of 8.1.2004, amending the Order on combating salmonella in laying hens, thus implementing the requirements of Directive 2002/4/EC.

audits.title: Residues and contaminants in live animals and animal products, including controls on veterinary medicinal products

recommendations.text: To ensure that targeting criteria are employed by official samplers in order to maximise the chances of detecting illegal use of banned substances and unauthorised use of licensed VMPs.

To ensure that official sampling is equally likely to be carried out on Fridays as on any other day of the week, in order to ensure that the requirements as regards the sampling strategy, laid down in Annex III of Council Directive 96/23/EC, are respected.

To ensure that the requirements of Article 4 of Council Directive 90/167/EEC regarding the production of medicated feedingstuffs using pre-mixes, are correctly applied to on-farm production of medicated feedingstuffs.
To take action to prevent the use of medicated pre-mixes for top dressing.

To ensure that the requirement in Article 66(2) of Council Directive 2001/82/EC, that retail distributors of VMPs record the manufacturer's batch number for each outgoing transaction is correctly transposed and fully implemented.

To ensure that all analytical methods used for residues are fit for purpose and validated to the standards laid down in Commission Decision 2002/657/EC, within the time limits laid down in that Decision.

To ensure that adequate resources are available for the execution of all NRL functions. 9. ADDENDUM In their fax of 2 July 2004 the Danish competent authorities provided an action plan addressing the above recommendations, as follows. Recommendation 1: The importance of following the existing instructions on targeting of samples will be stressed to the Official Veterinarians at the slaughterhouses. Recommendation 2: The importance of following the existing instructions on targeting of samples will be stressed to the Official Veterinarians at the slaughterhouses. That includes that samples must be taken at different intervals and not excluding certain weekdays, weeks or months. It will be included in the descriptions of the projects to be carried out in 2005 that samples must be taken with equal frequencies on every day of the 23 week including Friday. It will also be stressed that samples must be kept in a locked refrigerator/freezer until they are dispatched to the laboratory. Recommendation 3: Rules will be set up for the on-farm use of pre-mixes in compliance with the EU legislation, as quickly as possible. The plan is to examine the level of the actual use of these pre-mixes on farms, and if this use can be stopped. If not, an authorisation and control system will be set up for the on-farm production. Expected time frame is up to 1-2 years for the completion of these corrective actions, if a new authorisation system has to be set up. Recommendation 4: The marketing authorisation on premixes will be changed in order to be in compliance with the EU legislation. This will be completed within one year. Recommendation 5: The derogation in Article 66 (2) of Council Directive 2001/82/EC, is presently being transposed into Danish legislation, and will be in place no later that August 2004. Recommendation 6: With the increased staff asked for it should be possible to validate all the methods for Group A substances before 01-10-2005 and all methods for group B substances before 01-09-2007. (The Danish competent authorities already indicated their intention to make contracts with other laboratories with appropriately validated methods, pending completion of the validation work for Group A substances). Recommendation 7: In the next years the experience with the validations and the implementing of more methods will be used to evaluate the number of staff needed to ensure an adequate NRL-function after 2007.

audits.title: Animal Welfare at Slaughter

recommendations.text: Official veterinarians perform audits of the operators' own checks in slaughterhouses regarding animal welfare requirements in a uniform way (Article 3 and point 4 of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) n°882/2004).

The results of audits and inspections performed in slaughterhouses for animal welfare requirements are reported and recorded in databases in a uniform way so that the CA can evaluate and audit the results of the controls (Annex I, section II of Regulation (EC) n°854/2004 and point 4 of article 4 of Regulation (EC) n°882/2004).
Adequate training or guidelines are provided to the official veterinarians on how to perform complete controls at slaughter and killing in slaughterhouses (Article 6 of Regulation (EC) n°882/2004).
The ramps for unloading animals in slaughterhouses have a minimum slope (point 1 of chapter II of Annex A of Directive 93/119/EC).
Drinking water is available to animals which are not taken directly upon arrival to the place of slaughter (point 9 of chapter II of Annex A of Directive 93/119/EC).
Broilers are spared any avoidable excitement during lairaging in slaughterhouses (Article 3 of Directive 93/119/EC).
Animals are handled in slaughterhouses by people with the necessary knowledge and skill and are spared any avoidable excitement during movement (Articles 3 and 7 of Directive 93/119/EC).
Electrical stunning equipment has an audible or visible device indicating the length of time of its application to an animal (chapter II, A, 2 (b) of Directive 93/119/EC).
Back-up for stunning equipment is kept at the place of slaughter of the animals for emergency use (point 2 of Article 6 of Directive 93/119/EC).
Stunning equipment is maintained (point 1 of article 6 of Directive 93/119/EC).
Training of handlers is checked by official veterinarians (Article 7 of Directive 93/119/EC).
Official veterinarians determine the strength and duration of current used for waterbath stunner in poultry slaughterhouses (point II, 3, B, 1 of Annex C of directive 93/119/EC).
When concussion is used for stunning cattle, no fracture of the skull occurs (point 2. (a) of chapter II of Annex C of Directive 93/119/EC).

Documents and materials for contingency plans are reorganised to take account of the restructuring and the contingency plans for Avian Influenza and Newcastle Disease are updated (point 3 of Article 13 of Regulation (EC) n°882/2004). 22 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/8039/2006 With their comments on the draft version of this report, the CCA provided an action plan which addressed each of the recommendations. In particular, the CCA made the following commitments to improve the system of controls of animal welfare requirements in slaughterhouses and to correct the deficiencies identified in the different slaughterhouses visited: · Regardi n° 1, the DVFA will identify "animal welfare" as a separate area when drawing up the auditing guidelines for 2007, which will help to ensure that all animal welfare requirements are checked and complied with. Uniformity between the regional food and veterinary authorities will be achieved by issuing circulars and guidelines and holding meetings at which all inspection departments will be represented. The DVFA is planning to revise the guidelines on documentation of checks relating to animal welfare requirements at slaughterhouses by the end of 2006. In the letters addressed to the heads of the regional authorities on 1 June 2006, the DVFA highlighted the points to be followed for performing regular animal welfare audits and checks in slaughterhouses. · Regardi s n° 2 and n°3, the DVFA will ensure that checklists used in slaughterhouses are regularly updated and that check lists specific to animal welfare requirements at slaughterhouses are used during animal welfare inspections. Appropriate provisions on the stunning of animals will be included in the new guidelines on documentation of checks relating to animal welfare requirements at slaughterhouses and the previous outdated circular on stunning will be repealed before the end of 2006. In the letters addressed to the heads of the regional authorities on 1 June 2006, the DVFA highlighted the need for appropriate reporting and recording of the results of animal welfare audits and inspections. · Regardi n°3 on training, the DVFA will ensure regular training on animal welfare in slaughterhouses for all official veterinarians. In the letters addressed to the heads of the regional authorities on 1 June 2006, the DVFA indicated that a number of official veterinarians must be trained to carry out checks in relation to animal welfare requirements. · Regardi n° 4, in the letters addressed to the heads of the regional authorities on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests from the head of the region concerned that it should be ensured in connection with re-approval of the slaughterhouse that the slope of entry and exit ramps should be kept to the minimum possible. · Regardi n° 5, in the letters addressed to the heads of two regions concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests that the slaughterhouses be informed in writing that animals which are not taken directly to the place of slaughter must have access to drinking water and that compliance with this requirement must be checked. · Regardi n° 6, in a letter addressed to the head of the region concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests that it should be ensured that the slaughterhouse puts in place a procedure to avoid unnecessary excitement to the broilers kept in cages before slaughter and during washing at the slaughterhouse. 23 · Regardi n°7, in the letter addressed to the head of the region concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA request that it should be ensured that the slaughterhouse is informed in writing that animals must be handled by persons with the necessary knowledge and skills, and be spared any avoidable excitement during handling. · Regardi n° 8, the DVFA stated that the stunning device was fitted with visible signal and that the operator demonstrated to the mission team that the light lit up when there was current between electrodes in a bucket of water. · Regardi n° 9, in the letter addressed to the head of the regions concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests that it should be ensured that the back-up stunning equipment for emergency use must be at the place of slaughter when slaughtering is taking place. · Regardi n° 10, in the letter addressed to the head of the region concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests that it should be ensured that the stunning equipment is properly maintained. · Regardi n°11, in the letter addressed to the head of the region concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests that it should be ensured as soon as possible that the official veterinarian checks the training of personnel, including workers employed to handle animals. · Regardi n°12, in the letter addressed to the head of the region concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests that it should be ensured without delay that the official veterinarian determines the strength and duration of the current used for water bath stunner in poultry slaughterhouse. · Regardi n°13, the DVFA stated that during the mission calves were stunned by concussion and not adult cattle, which is normally slaughtered for halal slaughter and very rarely suffers skull damage after stunning by concussion. In the letter addressed to the head of the region concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests that the slaughterhouse be informed in writing that skull fractures must not occur when cattle is stunned by concussion, and that the concussion stunning equipment should not be used in the future on animals under the age of 12 month or bulls. · Regardi n° 14, the DVFA stated that Contingency plans had been amended to take into account the DVFA's most recent restructuring and that the operational plans for avian influenza and for Newcastle Disease will be amended respectively by 1 January 2007 and 31 December 2007. 24

responses.response: The reorganisation of the laboratory service has had an influence on the turnaround time in 2012 and partly in 2013. The analytical control of feed is now carried out at two laboratories, which guarantee that the capacity is adequate. In order to reduce the costs for the business operators, the analytical control is now organised so that the samples normally will be analysed in full series and not necessary on the day of arrival. This can prolong the turnaround time. The laboratory is also working on a new organisation of the sampling, which will reduce the turnaround time. Concerning screening methods for coccidiostats used in Denmark the situation in 2012 was that monensin, lasalocid, salinomycin and narasin/nicarbazin were used (Informations from Vetstat). audits.title: Fishery products

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls involve verification of compliance by the FBOs with their obligations, in order to comply with the requirements laid down in Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 27, 36 and 41. Associated findings Nos 20, 23, 24, 30 and 39.

citations.text: According to national procedure, FBOs do not have to document good manufacturing practices (GMPs) if they are not linked to food safety. Official assessment of GMPs, as required by Article 10.2.d of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, is restricted to the explanation of the modus operandi by FBOs to official inspectors. The audit team noted that in one of the establishments visited testing of ready-to-eat products was not documented. This lack of documentation had not been acted on by officials during previous control visits4.

In some cases, deficiencies noted by the audit team during the visits had already been identified during official controls or were detected by official inspectors during the Commission services visit (e.g. shortcomings on traceability or lack of temperature records). However, this was not always the case5, for example: Regarding general hygiene, in one establishment visited there was no physical separation (i.e. some space) between raw material and products ready to be smoked. Stagnant water on the floor after washing whole and gutted fish was also noted that could splash the products ready to be smoked which were kept nearby. In another two establishments visited protective clothes, including shoe protection, were used both inside and outside premises6. Regarding HACCP plans, in one establishment one process was not described in the plan; in another establishment the official inspector agreed with the audit team that the plan needed to be reviewed as it did not reflect the reality of production7. Regarding L. monocytogenes, in the establishments visited the audit team noted cases when the limit for L. monocytogenes in smoked products after their production was established at <10 cfu/g, the number of units comprising the sample was limited to one, testing of products was only carried out at the end of the shelf-life and never before the food left the immediate control of the FBO, frequencies described in the FBO procedures were not met and testing of equipment and surfaces was not included in the FBO's own-check plan8. 5 During the audit, the DVFA provided evidence of corrective actions already taken to correct some of these situations. 6 In their response to the draft report DVFA informed that this has also been followed up, so protective clothes are not used outdoors. This follow-up message was given orally. 7 In their response to the draft report DVFA noted that the HACCP plan shall according to the inspection frequency guidelines section 7 be inspected at least once every year (or every other year in elite establishments) at wholesalers, so the deficiencies would probably have been discovered during this control. The DVFA added that they will follow-up regarding the first establishment, so that all processes are included in the HACCP plan. For the second establishment, DVFA stated that they will ensure that the HACCP plan is reviewed to reflect the reality of the production. 8 In their response to the draft report DVFA noted that the limit for content of Listeria was corrected to "not detected in 25 g", that testing was started to be carried out before the food leaves the immediate control of the FBO, and the frequencies for control described in the FBO procedures were started to be met. Testing of equipment and surfaces were included in the FBOs own check plan. And, as the HACCP plan also had been effective in the other establishment, the DVFA had also accepted that the number of sample units could be 8 Regarding histamine, in one establishment visited the FBO did not carry out testing for histamine as it had requested the corresponding laboratory results from its supplier. However, these results comprised one sample instead of the nine required in Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, and the testing method was not the method foreseen in the same Regulation9. Regarding food additives, in one establishment visited an additive non- authorised in fresh fish fillets (E 500) was used; in other establishments, a mix of additives which composition was not clear was used to prevent melanosis in Norwegian lobster. In addition, in this case the instructions provided by the supplier differed from the instructions on the product label and from the FBO procedures. The FBO did not follow a procedure when using it (e.g. specific quantity to be used, the immersion time, etc.).

The audit team noted that most of the above problems arose as official controls were not carried out as a verification (i.e. checking by examination and the consideration of objective evidence) of compliance with the relevant FBO obligations; instead, these official controls were based on simple declarations by the individual FBOs on whether or not there was compliance with the said requirements.

Official controls on production and placing on the market cover all stages of production and are in general implemented in accordance with EU requirements. However, for certain requirements (e.g. use of food additives), officials over-rely on statements and declarations provided by FBOs without actually verifying actual compliance. Thus, in those cases official controls do not provide guarantees that fishery products and FBO comply with relevant Union requirements.

Testing for parasites takes place randomly by visual inspection. In addition, during official controls, official inspectors focus on FBO own-checks and, in particular, if fishery products are intended to be consumed raw or subject to any other treatment that is insufficient to kill viable parasites, FBOs must have adequate procedures in place. These procedures shall include freezing of fishery products derived from wild caught fish or, in the case of farmed fishery products, a certificate to guarantee the requirements of Section VII, Chapter III.D.3.d of Regulation (EC) No 853/200411. However the audit team noted that in one of the establishments visited producing smoked wild salmon, the official inspector had not detected that salmon was not being subjected to freezing at any stage of production12. 11 According to the information provided by DVFA, Danish farmed trout is exempted from complying with this requirement until 1 January 2018 based on a study carried out by the Laboratory of Aquatic Pathobiology, Department of Veterinary Diseases Biology, Faculty of Health Science, University of Copenhagen named "Development of certification methodology for Danish mariculture for use by relief from new EU freezing requirements (2014)". 12 In their response to the draft report DVFA noted that a follow-up on the matter has been made, so that there now are procedures in place that ensure that all wild salmon is frozen if they are to be consumed raw or almost raw. 10

Official controls of fishery products are carried out according to EU requirements. The weaknesses detected regarding official checks on the operators' control of parasites indicates that fishery products reach the market with insufficient treatment to kill viable parasites. 5.4 FOLLOW-UP OF RASFF NOTIFICATIONS Articles 50 and 52 of Section I, Chapter IV to Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Findings

At the opening meeting, DVFA provided information on the follow-up of four 2014 RASFF notifications, one related to one establishment and the other three related to another establishment. Regarding the first one, the L. monocytogenes strain was typed by whole-genome-sequencing and it was found that the L. monocytogenes type was identical to human isolates of listeria (involving mortality) and that this type had not, at that time, been seen in other samples from Danish establishments. Although the FBO revised the establishment's procedures, there was a new human outbreak in 2015 involving this specific L. monocytogenes type. Further measures have been taken by the FBO and, at the time of the audit, DVFA was monitoring them. Regarding the other three RASFF notifications, also involving L. monocytogenes, the follow-up focussed on the procedures in place by the FBO and the FBO's laboratory results. Advice concerning shelf-life labelling and monitoring was given by DVFA but no official samples to verify the FBO's laboratory results were taken (see paragraph 23 as part of the non- compliances described were seen in this establishment)14.

There is a system in place to investigate problems that occur and to take action in response to RASFF notifications. However, the over-reliance on statements and declarations provided by FBOs described in conclusion 27 has also had an adverse impact in the follow-up of RASFF notifications. 5.5 LABORATORIES Legal requirements Articles 11, 12 and 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 1 and 5 and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and Article 2 and Section II of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005. Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006. Regulation (EC) No 333/2007. Regulation (EU) No 589/2014. Findings

responses.response: od is defined in Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and includes water "intentionally incorporated into the food during its manufacture, preparation or treatment." I.e., water that is not incorporated into the food is not itself food. Since ice used for chilling fish is not incorporated into the fish it is not food, and companies producing ice solely for this purpose are not a food businesses. Therefore Companies producing ice solely for chilling fish are not registered as food businesses and the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration does not perform official controls in these companies. In order to fulfil the requirements in Annex II, Chapter VII, point 4, of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 the food business operator receiving ice for chilling fish must ensure that the ice is produced from potable water or clean water and is made, handled and stored before receipt in the food establishment under conditions that protect it from contamination. audits.title: evaluate the production and use of certain proteins of animal origin in feed for aquaculture animals

recommendations.text: ganise and carry out official controls on the new requirements concerning the use of PAP of non-ruminant origin in feed for aquaculture animals, as laid down by Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Recommendation based on conclusions: 10 and 19. Associated findings: 5, 6, 9, 12, 13, 14 and 17.

citations.text: In the slaughterhouse, in the processing plants and in the transporter visited, the audit team noted that, although checks on requirements of the ABP legislation were carried out during official controls, these had never included the specific requirements applicable to sourcing and transport of ABP to be used for the production of derogated PAP for aquaculture feeding. Moreover, it was noted that neither guidelines nor checklists were available to the inspectors to assist them in verifying compliance with these requirements. As a result, official controls overlooked a number of deficiencies (see points 11, 12 and 13). This is not in line with the requirements on official controls laid down in Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

Official controls in manufacturers of feed for aquaculture cover aspects related to the feed ban in general. A specific checklist, which includes feed ban related issues, is available, 4 although it is officially no longer in use because it needs to be updated in order to include the specific requirements for the use of derogated PAP for aquaculture feeding. In this respect, the audit team noted that some requirements related to operators' own checks and their procedures for sourcing eligible PAP had been overlooked during official controls (see points 14 and 17). This is not fully in line with the requirements on official controls laid down in Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

However, the audit team noted that the DVFA laboratory did not always use the Standard Operating Procedure describing the operational protocols for the combination of light microscopy and PCR, developed by the EURL-AP, although this procedure is a binding complement of the requirements laid down by Annex VI to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. All samples were first submitted to screening by the light microscopy method irrespective of the nature of the concerned sample. It was noted that aquaculture feed samples containing blood meal were not submitted to PCR, contrary to the aforementioned Standard Operating Procedure, because the light-microscopy method did not detect any particles from terrestrial origin. Following the audit and during the drafting of the report, the competent authority informed the audit team that the laboratory would now follow the above-mentioned Standard Operating Procedure. 5 Conclusions on official control systems

A system of official controls on the requirements concerning the ABP legislation and the general feed ban is in place in slaughterhouses, ABP plants, transporters of ABP and PAP and in feed manufactures producing feed for aquaculture animals. This also includes a sampling plan to detect ruminant DNA in feed for aquaculture animals. However, no specific checks on the new requirements pertaining to the use of derogated PAP in aquaculture feed have been organised yet. As a consequence, although the competent authorities undertook some immediate actions to address some of the issues identified, they are not yet in position to ensure that only eligible PAP is used for the production of feed for aquaculture animals. 5.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE IMPLEMENTATION OF FEED BAN REQUIREMENTS ALONG THE CHAIN Legal requirements Article 7 and Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, Article 21, 22, 45(1), 46, 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, Article 17(1) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011; Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Annex VI to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. 5.2.1 Origin of ABP and their processing into PAP

In one of the processing plants visited, the transport of ABP was outsourced to an external ABP transporter, who was also authorised to transport Category 2 and Category 3 ABP with no limitations in terms of animal species. This transporter was also providing the reusable containers. The audit team noted that the processing plant operator did not have any measures in place to ensure that the reusable containers were either dedicated exclusively for transport of eligible ABP or were cleaned by means of an authorised cleaning procedure prior to being used for the transport of ABP destined for production of 6 derogated PAP as required by Chapter IV, Section D, point (b) of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. This was not identified during official controls.

The audit team noted that in one of the two processing plants visited consignments of PAP were dispatched without the required warning sentence in the commercial documents, as laid down by Chapter IV, Section D, point (e) of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. This was not identified during official controls. 5.2.2 Use of PAP for producing compound feed

Both fish feed producers visited in Denmark were dedicated to the production of fish feed. According to the feed business operators, the only information required to their suppliers of PAP was an evidence of approval/registration in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and a written declaration of the origin of PAP in terms of animal species. The audit team noted that no further information to confirm the origin and the eligibility of the PAP had ever been requested by the feed business operators. This issue was not checked during official controls.

The fish feed manufacturers visited used labels on the products containing information in several languages. In order to accommodate the information required in all languages, the operators made use of very small fonts difficult to read. Moreover, it was noted that in feed containing fish meal and other PAP, the operators used at the same time the warning sentence required for fish meal and the one required for PAP. As a result there was a risk of misinterpretation because fish meal can be fed to all farmed animals except ruminants, whereas PAP can only be fed to aquaculture farmed animals. This issue was not checked during official controls. 5.2.3 Actions in case of non-compliance

Official controls carried out in slaughterhouses, ABP plants, transporters of ABP and PAP and in feed manufactures producing feed for aquaculture animals, do not yet include regular checks on the new requirements pertaining to the use of derogated PAP in aquaculture feed. This limits the ability of the competent authorities to ensure that only eligible PAP is used for the production of feed for aquaculture animals. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system of official controls already in place in slaughterhouses, ABP plants, transporters of ABP and PAP and in feed manufacturers producing feed for aquaculture animals has not been extended yet to include the requirements related to the use of derogated PAP. Although the competent authority undertook some immediate actions to address some of the shortcomings identified during the audit, the ability of the competent authorities to ensure that only eligible PAP is used for the production of feed for aquaculture animals, is still limited. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 04 February 2015 with representatives of the central competent authority and of the meat inspection team of the slaughterhouse visited. At this meeting, main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. The central competent authorities did not indicate any disagreement with these. 8 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendation set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. No. Recommendation 1. To organise and carry out official controls on the new requirements concerning the use of PAP of non-ruminant origin in feed for aquaculture animals, as laid down by Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. recommendations.text: The CA should update the official sheep flock register so that it contains all the information required by Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 21/2004, in particular the name of transporter, the registration number of the part of the means of transport carrying the animals and date of identification of born animals. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 63. Associated findings Nos. 22 and 57.

citations.text: The CA has designed a template for holding register for sheep to be used by the farmer. Not all data required by EU legislation are included in the template, e.g. the result and date of last inventory, the name of transporter, the registration number of the vehicle or date of identification of new-born animals. On the sheep farm visited by the audit team those data (with exception of the result and date of last inventory) were not recorded by the keeper. This is not in line with Article 5 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 21/2004. 5.1.3 Correspondence with reality

On a sheep farm visited, all animals, including lambs for slaughter were tagged with two earmarks, one of them electronic. The flock register was updated in a timely manner by the owner. But not all data required by the EU legislation were included (for more see point 22). The sheep off movements were notified in a timely manner to the CHR (as batch movement). The result of the latest animal inventory was updated into the CHR in January 2016, but the number of animals recorded was significantly lower than the number of animals present on the farm at the time of audit team visit. The reason provided for the discrepancy was a mistake made by farmer's consultant when updating the CHR. 17 Conclusions on data quality

The incomplete official template for flock register on sheep farms has no big impact in the day-to-day business (small sheep population) but could delay traceability in the case of emergencies (e.g. Foot-and-Mouth disease outbreak).

recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that certifying officers certify only data of which they have personal knowledge or which can be ascertained by them as required by point 2, Article 3 of Directive 96/93/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 89. Associated finding No. 74.

citations.text: At the assembly centre visited, the audit team noted shortcomings related to the certification procedures, in particular that the official veterinarian accepted incomplete information or unsigned statements by the owners of the animals. Furthermore, the farmers' statements that animals stayed for 30 days in their holding (for pigs) and no 20 animals were imported during the same period (for pigs and bovines) were directly accepted as the basis for certification without any additional verification (e.g. validated against data in the CHR)1. This is not in line with point 2, Article 3 of Directive 96/93/EC. The same shortcomings were detected during an internal audit in 2012, but no actions have been implemented yet by the CA to address them. 5.2.2 Fitness for purpose

The central database is only partially used for certification purposes; instead the certification at assembly centres relies on a system of pre-certification statements, some of which are not verified as should be. As a result, the existing weaknesses negatively affect reliability of the certification process for intra-EU trade. 5.3 MONITORING AND REVIEW Compliance with minimum legal requirements requires significant investments but doesn't guarantee efficient and effective functionalities for the various use-cases. In order to bring the systems up to a level where users get real benefits and return for investment, more than minimum compliance is needed. Review and continuous improvement are the mechanisms, which ensure that users receive a good quality of service, and the system continues to deliver efficiently and effectively what is expected from it. For the purposes of this audit, four elements of monitoring and review were assessed: Monitoring of control results for: o FBO compliance levels, types of non-compliance and trends; o Verifying effectiveness of controls and further development; Analysis of existing data for various purposes; Internal and external audits or other evaluations. Legal requirements Monitoring of control results: Commission Decision 2008/654/EC provides guidance on the annual report for the single integrated multiannual control plan. Point 9.2.2 of the Annex to this Decision suggests that control data should be analysed, patterns and trends identified and root causes for non-compliance described, as appropriate. Article 4.2 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 has a generic requirement: "The Competent Authorities shall ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness official controls on live animals..." Article 8.3 of the same Regulation requires Competent Authorities to "have procedures in place to verify the effectiveness of official controls that they carry out..." Monitoring of control results is one way of addressing the latter requirement ­ other means do exist but those fall outside the scope of this audit. 23 There is no explicit legal requirement in the specific IRS legislation to monitor, review and improve the systems. Equally, analysis of existing data for various purposes is not a legal requirement ­ this audit attempted to harvest good/best practice in this area, if possible. Internal and external audits or other evaluations: Article 4.6 of Regulation (EC) 882/2004 requires that Competent Authorities "...carry out internal audits or have external audits carried out, and shall take appropriate measures in the light of their results..." Recommendation based on conclusions: 74 Associated findings: 68 To ensure that BIPs comply with approval requirements of Decision 2001/812/EC including hygiene requireme based on conclusions: 24 Associated findings: 16 To provide LVUs with instructions as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 to ensure that all required data is entered in to TRACES especially in the context of incoming notifications which require confirmation that appropriate follow-up has been implemented; e.g confirmation of receipt at destinatio based on conclusions: 85 Associated findings: 82 and 83

citations.text: Regarding both products of animal origin and products of non-animal origin, if the result shows a non-compliance, the consignment is rejected and can be destroyed or re- dispatched. In the case of re-dispatch, the DVFA requires confirmation from the country of destination that they agree to receive non-compliant consignments as required by Article 21 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. A 60-day deadline is given to food business operators to destroy or re-dispatch non-compliant consignments. The audit team noted that where the consignment of products of non-animal origin is re-dispatched, the importer is not required to submit evidence to ensure that the 60-day limit is respected as foreseen in Article 21(2) of Regulation 882/2004. The DVFA stated that in the case of destruction, the importer submits proof of the destruction of the rejected consignment in accordance with Article 20(2) of Regulation 882/2004.

Where a rejected consignment of products of non-animal origin is re-dispatched, the operator is not requested to submit any evidence that the consignment left Denmark for an approved destination. This does not ensure that the deadline established in EU legislation has been respected and opens up the possibility that the consignment may have been illegally placed on the EU market. 13

audits.title: Animal welfare - tail-docking of pigs

recommendations.text: The competent authority should provide inspectors with suitable compliance 2. criteria to enable them to effectively enforce legal requirements of Council Directive 2008/120/EC and Council Directive 98/58/EC that are related to risk factors for tail-biting. Conclusion 50. Findings 39, 45. The competent authority should provide inspectors with suitable instructions and guidance to be enable them to enforce the provision on the prevention of tail- biting and avoidance of routine tail-docking, as laid down in the second paragraph of point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I of Council Directive 2008/120/EC, including how they should assess evidence of tail and ear lesions on farm and what constitutes sufficient measures by farmers to change inadequate environmental 5. conditions or management systems before resorting to tail-docking of pigs. This entails the development of measurable criteria to enable inspectors to properly assess progress with regard to the risk factors listed in the new DVFA guidelines on enrichment materials and the avoidance of tail-docking. Conclusion 51. Findings 39 and 44 to 46. The competent authority should, as required by Article 3(a) of Regulation 882/2004, take account of identified risks such as the level of non-compliance in herds with slaughter pigs compared to sow herds and post-mortem data on tail damage at slaughter to further target herds with slaughter pigs and improve risk factors for tail-biting on these premises. Conclusion 51. Finding 46. Conclusion 52. Findings 47 to 49. The competent authority should continue to work with private veterinarians to maximise the impact of Veterinary Advisory Service Contracts and ensure that priorities set in herd action plans support farmers in their assessment of risk factors as well as other relevant data related to the need for tail-docking, as required by point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I of Council Directive 2008/120/EC. Conclusion 31. Findings 24 to 26. The competent authority should consider liaising with other Government Agencies responsible for funding new buildings where pigs are to be kept and renovating existing ones with the assistance of European funding under Article 17 of Regulation (EU) No 1305/2013 to ensure not only that payments related to such facilities are suitable to commitments going beyond the relevant mandatory standards where they are related to animal welfare but that in general all funded facilities, as a minimum, comply with relevant mandatory requirements (of Directives 2008/120/EC and 98/58/EC) including the avoidance of routine tail- docking e.g. slurry systems that can handle optimal enrichment materials, different temperature zones, suitable flooring, feeding, space allowances etc. Conclusions 35, 36. Findings 33, 34.

responses.response: The guideline for animal welfare controls in pig herds and/or the guideline on enrichment material will be updated to include liance criteria for air quality, feeding space, and drinkers. It will at the same time be considered, whether an update on the compliance criteria concerning mixing of pigs, which are already in the guideline, is appropriate. This update is expected to be finalised during the first half of 2018. An update of the guideline on animal welfare controls in pig herds to include compliance criteria for staff will have to wait the adoption of an order, which requires that the person responsible for a pig herd of a certain size shall have relevant training. This update is expected to be finalised during the second half of 2018.

recommendations.text: Ensure that CBs are subject to appropriate supervision by the CA and 2. appropriate coordination between CA and CBs is in place in line with Articles 3. 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 15, 32. 4. Associated findings No 13, 14, 25, 27-31. Ensure that official controls cover the monitoring of the use of registered names to describe products place on the market in line with Article 36(3)(b) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 23. Associated findings No 19. Ensure that all elements of Product Specifications are checked during official controls, and in particular: The compliance of labelling with Article 12(3) and 23(2) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 and That a calculation of the input/output is performed (Article 4 of Regulation (EU) No 668/2014). Recommendation is based on conclusion No 32. Associated findings No 27. Ensure that enforcement measures imposed are sufficiently dissuasive to reduce the risk of non-compliant PDO/PGI/TSG reaching the market. Recommendation is based on conclusion No 39. Associated findings No 38.

citations.text: At the time of the audit, the CA and CBs were in the process of defining the respective conditions and responsibilities which will eventually be part of the control plan. However, the control plan was in the early stages of preparation and the concept of supervision of the CBs by the CA had not been entirely worked out by the CA. Consequently, supervision of CBs by the CA was not yet in place. During inspections observed (see chapter 5.2.4), the audit team was informed by a CB inspector that the correct approach to controlling certain elements of the Product Specification was not 4 clear for the inspector. This lack of supervision by the CA was giving rise to uncertainty on what should be included in the official controls by CBs and risks non-compliant PGI being placed on the market. This is not in line with Article 5(2)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

There was evidence of lack of coordination between the CA, the CBs and Producers/Processors. As an example, during one site visit, a CB had not issued an inspection report for the most recent official control undertaken prior to this audit. According to the CB inspector this lack of reporting was due to unresolved contractual issues which prevented her from completing the official control. The CA contradicted the inspector. Nevertheless, the producer continued to sell the PGI using the protected name and Union symbol. It became clear to the audit team, that none of the key players were fully aware that this non-compliant situation existed until the time of the audit. This is not in line with Article 5(2)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which requires that there is efficient and effective coordination between the delegating CA and the CB. Conclusions on Control Bodies

At the time of the audit, supervision of CBs by CAs was not implemented and there was a lack of coordination between the key players involved in official controls. 5.2.3 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Articles 37(1) and 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

At the time of the audit, a second CB had not issued any report for the official control of one PGI. Nevertheless, the producer continued to sell the PGI using the protected name and Union symbol. The CB inspector stated that a report had not been issued as there 6 was no written agreement with the Producer group in place at the time of the audit. The CB stated that a verbal agreement was in place and legally this was considered as a contract. The CA had granted the CB an approval to operate on the understanding that there was an agreement (whether verbal or written) between the Producer group and the CB. This situation highlighted a lack of coordination between the key players involved (see also paragraph 14). (b) Performance of Official Control Activities at Visited Premises

However, the following weaknesses were noted: Although the inspectors noted some labelling non-compliances, the full extent of the labelling requirements (Article 12(3) and 23(2) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012) were not fully implemented at the time of the audit. (see further details under this chapter, point (c) Labelling ­ correct use of Union symbol and presentation of the protected name). There was no verification of the of input/output calculations performed by the operator. This is not in line with Article 4 of Regulation (EU) No 668/2014.

The CB inspector met at one premises queried the exact meaning of some elements of the Product Specification. The CB inspector raised issues1 in relation to carrying out official controls in an effective manner. The preparation of the control plan by this CB had identified these issues as a challenge that needed clarification from the CA. (c) Labelling ­ correct use of Union symbol and presentation of the protected name

During the audit, there were numerous instances of non-compliances relating to the proper use of the Union symbol and the protected name. The ensuing discussion between the CB, CA, the producer and the audit team illustrated the challenge associated with labelling and the different interpretations that exists. It became clear that there is a need of guidance on labelling to be available to producers and CBs.

One of the inspections observed was the first official control of a particular PGI which constituted the verification of the Product Specification prior to placing the product on the market. In this instance, the operator had a model of the labelling intended to be used on the final product. The inspector briefly reviewed this information, but stressed that it was not the inspector's responsibility to approve labelling. In fact the labelling did not fully comply with the minimum requirements of the legislation, and in particular Article 12(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2014. 1 In their response to the draft report the CA noted that issues relating to the exact geographical location had been resolved after completion of the audit. 7

It was noted by the audit team that the Union symbol and the protected name were not always sufficiently close together to clearly link these two elements in the same field of vision. There were also examples of the protected name being misspelt, the Union symbol being less than 15 mm as well as other descriptive information contained in the Product Specification being incorrectly presented on the label. The CB inspectors observed did not detect all of the labelling non-compliances. Conclusions on Procedures and Performances of Official Control Activities

Although the CB inspectors were knowledgeable, there was a lack of guidance relating to the interpretation of the PDO/PGI/TSG legislation and its application in practice. This resulted in a number of deficiencies being overlooked by the inspectors. 5.2.5 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

responses.response: In order to ensure appropriate coordination between CA and CBs and to ensure sufficient coordination with other key players, the DVFA will: Assess the control plans submitted by the CBs in order to ensure that the control plans are fully in line with the requirements. recommendations.text: The CCA should ensure that RTE food establishments are approved for the 2. activities they actually carry out, that approval is adequately kept under review and that the list of approved establishments is kept up to date in order to comply with the requirements of Article 31 (2)(c), (e) and (f) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion No 36 Associated findings Nos 29, 30, 31, 35. The CCA should ensure that: official controls over FBOs' prevention measures for cross- contamination hazards are adequate and appropriate documents and records are kept by the FBOs in line with Article 5(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 to demonstrate the effective application of the HACCP principles, official controls verify the FBO's relevant records in line with Article 4(8)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion No 104. Associated findings Nos 61, 62, 63, 64. The CCA should ensure that official controls organised in such a way as to 4. adequately cover FBOs compliance with all the relevant EU legislation and that non-compliances detected are adequately classified taking into account risks related to RTE products. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 103, 107. Associated findings Nos 55, 59. In order to allow monitoring of corrective actions and, where appropriate initiation of enforcement, the CCA should ensure that non-compliances detected are systematically recorded and in particular that the relevant CCA procedures are consistently followed by the CA staff. Recommendation based on conclusion No 107. Associated findings Nos 54, 55.

citations.text: The audit team noted several discrepancies between the activities indicated on the list of approved food establishments, the activities mentioned in the approval certificates and the activities actually carried out in the establishments visited.

In some of the establishments visited the audit team noted that: the establishments had not been approved for all the activities which were actually carried out (e.g. fishery products establishment producing fried chicken skin was not approved as a poultry meat products establishment; a catering establishment cooking fish (among other activities) was not approved as a fishery products establishment). the establishments were listed under several activities which were not being carried out, or for which they have not been approved. one of the establishments visited was approved as a meat products establishment, but was not on the published list of approved food establishments.

These findings are not in compliance with the requirements of Article 31(2)(c) and (e) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which requires that the CA shall approve an establishment for the activities concerned and shall keep the approval under review when carrying out official controls.

Although the CA inspectors are required to verify the maintenance of approval conditions at least annually during inspection and the inspectors should update the relevant information in the KOR system (Control Objects Register ­the main database used by the CA for individual risk characterisation of each establishment), the audit team noted that it is not consistently carried out. As the published list of approved establishments obtains the information from KOR, the list is not up to date. Conclusion on registration/approval of food business operators
