audits.title: Official controls on imports of animals and goods

recommendations.text: To ensure that for consignments intended for ship supply, a CVED is issued at the BIP of entry for each consignment, i.e. for each certificate issued in the third country of origin, in accordance with the requirements of Article 3, 4 and 5 of Directive 97/78/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion: 64 Associated finding: 40

citations.text: The procedure applied in one seaport BIP in case of direct movement from the BIP to ship supply or to further storage facilities - one CVED for several consignments (and several veterinary certificates) in one means of transport - is not in line with the requirements of Directive 97/78/EC. On arrival at the BIP, consignments accompanied with several certificates, transported in the same means of transport were presented at the BIP by the operator with one CVED only. Consequently, not all certificates and not all commodities were mentioned on the CVED and thereafter recorded in TRACES.

The implementation of the import controls on animals, food and feed of animal origin and of goods subject to special import conditions is generally in line with EU legislation. The competent authorities ensure that documentary, identity and physical checks on animals and goods are carried out as required and that only compliant goods may be imported into the EU. Regular checks of airplane/shipping manifests contribute to ensuring that consignments requiring veterinary import controls do not escape such controls. Some weaknesses were noted in the documentary checks on re- imported consignments (for which the DVFA initiated corrective action) and those intended for ship supply, which weakens the requisite health guarantees and the traceability of consignments, respectively.

responses.response: With reference to the comments provided by the DVFA to finding icate number 40, the DVFA will stress to importers and the official ments inspectors at the BIPs, the importance of recording all health certificate numbers and commodities in the CVED. Furthermore, the DVFA will focus on ensuring receipt of confirmation from the captain of the ship within the time limit. Procedures for contacting the Customs authority in cases of missing reply will be added to the national guideline for control of ship supply. Page: 1

recommendations.text: To ensure that the sampling of animals on farms is targeted in accordance with the requirements laid down by part 2.3.2.1 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion No 22. Associated finding No 16.

citations.text: At the DVFA local branches visited and during field visits, the audit team interviewed the inspectors on the criteria for the selection of targeted samples. The inspectors met stated that the choice of the farms to be sampled was mainly based on the farm profile and the size and even information on the use of veterinary medicinal products available via VetStat could be consulted. In many cases, the inspectors stated that the samples on the farms would be taken randomly thus underestimating the importance of targeted sampling, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in points 2.1 and 2.3.2.1 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC). This situation was also observed during the 2010 audit and led to a recommendation. The audit team noted that the DVFA procedure did contain adequate guidance on the criteria to be used for the selection of targeted samples and that the procedure was accessible to the inspectors (see finding 12), though not all of the inspectors interviewed by the audit team were aware of the procedure.

The residue monitoring plan is generally implemented in accordance with planned arrangements. recommendations.text: To ensure that information regarding stability of analyte(s) in relevant matrices is included in validation of analytical methods in accordance with the requirements laid down in part 3.1.1.4 of Annex I to Decision 2002/657/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion No 37. Associated findings No 31(e).

citations.text: The audit team visited all three laboratories and noted that: a. All the laboratories were accredited to ISO 17025:2005 by the Danish Accreditation Fund (DANAK); b. The laboratories' facilities, equipment and staffing levels were adequate and the staff met were competent; c. A Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for reception of samples was in place, the criteria for accepting samples were recorded, and a procedure for sample rejection was available and followed; 7 d. The sensitivity of the analytical methods in use was sufficient to ensure the detection and quantification of residues of pharmacologically active substances at the Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs) listed in Table 1 of the Annex to Regulation (EU) No 37/2010, Minimum Required Performance Levels laid down in Article 4 and Annex II to Decision 2002/657/EC or, for unauthorised substances, the EURL recommended concentrations; e. At the DVFA laboratory in Ringsted and the DTU laboratory, the general SOP on validation of chemical methods of analysis included the assessment of all method performance parameters as required in Article 3 of Decision 2002/657/EC, with the exception of analyte stability. Whilst data on analyte stability in stock solutions were available, information regarding stability of analytes in relevant matrices had never been collected and evaluated as required in point 3.1.1.4 of the Annex to Decision 2002/657/EC. Reasonably short and largely adhered to turnaround times of 5 working days for antibiotics and 20 working days for the majority of pharmacologically active substances mitigate the possible effect of analyte instability in different matrices. f. Control charts (run for several parameters) were maintained and regularly checked (apart from the DVFA laboratory in Århus, see finding 34(b)) for long term trends in method performance. This fully satisfies the requirements of Article 5 of Decision 2002/657/EC. g. The laboratories regularly participated in relevant proficiency tests. Most of the results seen were satisfactory. When questionable results were obtained, adequate root-cause-analysis was carried out and appropriate corrective measures have been implemented.

Notwithstanding some minor shortcomings in method validation, the competent authority can have confidence in the laboratory performance and the reliability of analytical results. 5.2. Veterinary medicinal products 5.2.1. Competent authorities

audits.title: Live bivalve molluscs

recommendations.text: To classify production areas in line with Articles 52(2) and 52(3), 53(2) and 53(5), 54(3) and 55(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 30 and 31. Associated findings Nos 10, 11 and 18.

citations.text: Half of the active production areas (around 30 production areas in 2021) have a permanent classification. However, the remaining active production areas (or parts of them) are classified on a weekly basis (see Appendix 1 for further details) based on single results instead of on data from a review period, which is contrary to Article 52(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The same system (permanent and non-permanent classification) applies to aquaculture farms.

Regarding the production areas and aquaculture farms with permanent classification: · The competent authority has fixed a review period of three years for sampling data in order to determine compliance with the requirements for class A, B and C areas, as required in Article 52(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. · According to national legislation, the DVFA can classify production areas and aquaculture farms only if there are at least 24 analytical results in the previous three years, as foreseen in the community guide 7 and in the guidance document of the European Union Reference Laboratory (EURL) for monitoring bacteriological and viral contamination of bivalve molluscs 8. · Every year (except in two occasions in the last 15 years), the DTU carries out the assessment of the results of the previous three years and proposes the classification of each production area and aquaculture farm. 6 In their response to the draft report, the DVFA added that this structure has existed for several years and is latest confirmed by the main agreement between DTU and DVFA, dated l5th of October 2021, and by the document "COMMUNITY REFERENCE LABORATORIES/NATIONAL REFERENCE LABORATORIES (EU 625/2017), Member State: DENMARK, Rev. October 2021". 7 Community guide to the principles of good practice for the microbiological classification and monitoring of bivalve mollusc production areas (Issue 3, January 2017), available at https://ec.europa.eu/food/system/files/2018- 12/biosafety_fh_guidance_community_guide_bivalve_mollusc_monitoring_en.pdf. 8 The guidance document of the EU Reference Laboratory for monitoring bacteriological and viral contamination of bivalve molluscs ("Good Practice Guide; issue 7", December 2018). 5 · Once per year, the competent authority updates the list of production areas and aquaculture farms with permanent classification at the DVFA's website (available at https://www.foedevarestyrelsen.dk/Leksikon/Sider/Produktionsområder%20med%20 permanent%20mikrobiologisk%20klassificering.aspx), as required in Article 66(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The audit team noted that: · Following an agreement between the DVFA and the DTU, the classification of a production area applies to all molluscs' species available in that production area. Results from different molluscs' species are used for achieving the required 24 results. However, results from hand-picked samples that are collected closer to the shore, are excluded due to the higher level of contamination observed (see paragraph 12). Sanitary surveys highlight this different pattern in contamination and recommend the segregation of the corresponding (closer to the shore) parts, but the DVFA has not followed this recommendation. · The majority of the results considered for the classification of production areas are from harvesters' own-check plans. In the case of "opening samples" (five samples taken on the same day from the same harvesting ground, see Appendix 1) all five results are taken into account for making up the 24 results. This may give a non- adequate view of the E. coli variation in time, affecting therefore the accuracy of classification. · National legislation establishes that an appropriate number of samples have to be taken continuously in the previous 12 months. The DVFA considers that one analytical result in the previous 12 months is sufficient to keep the permanent classification of a production area and aquaculture farm9, which diverges from the recommendations of the above mentioned Community and EURL guides. · National legislation establishes a minimum frequency of sampling for keeping certain classification: every four weeks for class A areas, every thirteen weeks for class B and every six months for C, which for class B and C diverges from the recommendations of the above mentioned Community and EURL guides. · Contrary to Article 52(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, a production area can have more than one classification within it. Namely, if a sample ta

The DVFA has a yearly project to verify the reliability of harvesters' results. This project consists of a reduced number of samples (30 per year for biotoxins and toxin- producing plankton; 60 for E. coli 12) that officials take at the same location and moment than harvesters, following the corresponding DVFA sampling protocols. The audit team noted that: · The audit evaluated a case with discrepancies between the two results, with official results higher than operators' results. The DVFA disregarded the results from its official samples and used the harvesters lower results for action or decision (see paragraph 19). This makes the entire verification project of no value. In addition, the DVFA does not carry out an assessment of the discrepant results to check, for example, a correspondence with particular samplers. 12 According to the data provided, harvesters analysed around 950 samples E. coli in 2020, 470 toxin-producing plankton and 670 for biotoxins. 10 · According to the project, officials take five samples for E. coli testing from each production area to mirror the harvesters' sampling (i.e. five samples every time), which reduces the temporal official data available. · Results from official testing for biotoxins show that two or three samples from the same location are often taken, resulting also in a reduction of the temporal official data available.

The temporary classification of production areas (or parts of them) and the permanent classification of production areas are not in line with EU requirements. Therefore, the system does not ensure proper classification of production areas (or their parts) and there is a risk of live bivalve molluscs with an inadequate level of E. coli contamination for direct consumption reaching the market, which is a potential threat for food safety.

The DVFA does not follow the sanitary surveys' recommendations for sampling points and has not established a monitoring programme following them. Consequently, the validity of the sampling points for microbiological quality and their representativeness for production areas is questionable and so is the classification of production areas.

responses.response: These recommendations have caused the DVFA to initialize work to reconsider the use of Sanitary Survey's, including the use of fixed sampling points and the set-up of monitoring of production areas used for classifications. This is done in collaboration with DTU and AU. The DVFA expects this process to complete within 2022.

As required by Article 56(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the DVFA has completed sanitary surveys for all of the production areas (this is one of the two recommendations of the previous audit report still pending). By request of the DVFA, the DTU has carried out sanitary surveys, grouping all the production areas according to the water basins where they are located (fourteen sanitary surveys in total), and has published them on its website. The DTU plans to revise all sanitary surveys in a 5-year period (2021-2025). The audit team noted that: · The DTU informed that the revision will not include all the content but most of it and that it does not plan to carry out annual reviews (recommended by the EURL guidance document to ensure that the environmental conditions have not changed). · The DTU expects certain changes (inclusion or exclusion of areas/new areas) during the revision of some of the sanitary surveys to ensure that sanitary surveys are representative of the area considered, as required in Article 58 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. However, there are no clear procedures in place to ensure that a sanitary survey is completed before new areas are classified (see also paragraph 10 regarding temporary classification of production areas), contrary to what is required by Article 56(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. · The audit team reviewed a few sanitary surveys and noted that they are well structured and contain, in general, the elements required by legislation. However, the 7 DTU confirmed that it does not carry out any sampling to confirm the significance of the points selected, which can diminish the accuracy of the surveys. · The DVFA does not follow the recommendations from sanitary surveys regarding the location of sampling points for E. coli sanitary surveys; therefore the DVFA cannot ensure that sampling results are representative of the production area concerned. · The DVFA does not follow other recommendations from sanitary surveys either (e.g. the segregation or exclusion of a production area due to the different microbiological patterns observed). This can have an impact as, according to national legislation, harvesting should not take place near dumping areas, wastewater discharges, harbours, marinas or in areas affected by pollutants that can cause a deterioration of the sanitary quality of shellfish; however, it does not provide specific details on what size the exclusion zone must.

Contrary to Article 59 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the DVFA does not monitor production areas to check the microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs, the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water and the biotoxins and chemical contaminants in live bivalve molluscs.
Consequently, contrary to Article 61(1), the DVFA does not draw up sampling plans for the purpose of the checks mentioned in the previous point.
Very significant deficiencies of the official control system control weaken the ability of the authorities to ensure that bivalve molluscs harvested in Denmark are safe for the consumers.

The DVFA does not monitor production areas (and consequently has not drawn up sampling plans) to check the microbiological quality of bivalve molluscs, the presence of toxin-producing plankton in seawater, and the presence of biotoxins and heavy metals in bivalve molluscs. This poses a risk that live bivalve with high levels of E. coli contamination, or with biotoxins and heavy metals content above the regulated limits, might be placed on the market.

responses.response: The DVFA disagrees with the statements in No 14 and 32 regarding the lack of monitoring of production areas. The DVFA does monitor production areas for the presence of E. coli. However, recognizes that a sampling plan with fixed, sampling points has not been carried out, as SANTE F asks for, see response to recommendation 2. The DVFA direct the attention to article 57 in 627/2019, which stipulates that the competent authority shall ensure that the number of samples, the geographical distribution of sampling points and the sampling frequency for the programme shall ensure that the results of the analysis are representative of the area in question, not fixed. However, the DVFA believes that the Danish system delivers safe bivalve molluscs to the market. The DVFA will reconsider the use of Sanitary Survey's, the use of data and the set-up of monitoring of production areas; see the response to recommendations 1 and 2. recommendations.text: To ensure that the authority takes into account the results of checks carried out by food business operators or organisations representing food business operators, only when the conditions of Article 65(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 are fulfilled. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 28, 33. Associated findings Nos 6, 16 and 17.

citations.text: Article 65 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 allows competent authorities to take into account the results of checks carried out by food business operators or organisations when deciding on classification, reclassification, opening and closures if, among other requirements, the competent authority designates the laboratories carrying out the tests. However, contrary to this Article, the DVFA has not designated the laboratories carrying out the analysis for harvesters. In Denmark, national legislation requires that harvesters carry out sampling and testing where they intend to harvest and the DVFA bases all its decisions mostly on the harvesters' results (although the DVFA verifications samples described in paragraph 18 are also included for permanent classification). Harvesters can choose any of the private laboratories with a contract with the DVFA. These private laboratories operate under the same conditions described in paragraph 5. The audit team intended to review the laboratory that carried out all testing for harvesters in the years 2019 and 2020, but this laboratory refused the meeting and the DVFA did not have access to it either. This laboratory reported 4,300 biotoxins results for the regulated toxin groups (from approximately 670 samples), and 950 E. coli results. According to some of the laboratory reports available, E. coli testing was subcontracted to a laboratory that used an accredited method but there was no further information available regarding this laboratory (e.g. name, location, analytical method used, etc.). In 2021, harvesters decided to change the laboratory.

As envisaged in national legislation, the DVFA bases the control system of bivalve molluscs on harvesters' own-checks results (see Appendix 1 for further details). The audit team noted the following regarding this part of national legislation: · The conditions for sampling and transport of samples for E. coli testing are not in line with ISO 6887-3, which may compromise the quality of samples (i.e. storage of samples at up to 15ºC instead of 10 ºC, 48 hours instead of 24 to start the analyses of samples, etc.), and samples are not labelled at the point of collection. As a consequence, their legal, scientific and technical validity cannot be ensured, contrary to Article 34(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. · Regarding the conditions for sampling for toxin-producing plankton testing: For qualitative purposes, it consists of the pulling of a 20 microns mesh diameter net, three times vertically from the bottom to the surface. This method is adequate for qualitative purposes as it filters larger amounts of water and, therefore, concentrates the number of plankton cells. However, the 8 fact that the vessels are not in movement when samples are collected may diminish the performance of this method. For quantitative purposes, it requires the use of Niskin-like bottles, which might not allow the collection of a representative sample of the water column required in to Article 61(7) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. · It requires that samples for toxin-producing plankton are taken at the same location as samples for biotoxins, being therefore of limited value as early warnings suggesting an accumulation of biotoxins, and not representative of the areas concerned, contrary to Article 61(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. · It groups production areas for toxin-producing plankton sampling so harvesters have to take only one sample in any of the production areas constituting the group. However, the audit team noted some cases of very different results of samples taken on the same day in different production areas within the same group, which demonstrates that areas are not correctly grouped. · It requires weekly sampling of seawater for toxin-producing plankton testing except from November to March, when it can be done fortnightly. The weekly periodicity is adequate but the evidence presented to support fortnightly sampling does not provide a robust basis for this decision: the data evaluated are from 1991 to 2007 therefore the situation may have changed since then; the DVFA submitted a document that highlights the abundance of cysts of PSP producing plankton spp10. Therefore, peaks of plankton preceding biotoxin episodes can go unnoticed in between two samplings if they are taken 14 days apart. · It indicates that samples are normally heat-treated11 before being tested. This heat treatment, which takes place at organisations' premises, can lead to an unknown underestimation in the quantity of biotoxins present in the original sample and undermines their legal, scientific and technical validity, contrary to Article 34(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. · It requires weekly sampling of bivalve molluscs for biotoxins testing except for PSP from October to March, when the sampling frequency can be lower depending on DVFA decision. However, the DVFA did not provide a risk assessment with robust basis for this possibility to reduce the frequency of PSP testing. 5.1.3 Decisions after monitoring/decisions by the competent authority

As the DVFA does not carry out official monitoring of production areas, it does not take any decision in line with Article 62 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. All the decisions the DVFA took were based on harvesters' own-checks results (harvesters take samples in 10 In their response to the draft report, the DVFA confirmed that the possibility of fortnightly sampling has never been used. 11 In their response to the draft report, the DVFA clarified that is not the case of samples from line cultures and one of the ones from primary producers. 9 production areas and in aquaculture farms and, based on the analytical results, the DVFA opens production areas or aquaculture farms for harvesting with certain classification (see Appendix 1 for further details)). Article 65(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 allows the use of food business operators' results for the purpose of deciding on the classification, reclassification, opening or closure of production areas under certain conditions, but the system in Denmark does not meet them. The audit team noted the following that limit the reliability of harvesters' results: · The DVFA does not carry out training, inspection or supervision of harvesters taking samples (other than a visit to five samplers per year focussing on the ones from which samples are suspected to have hygiene problems or with remarks on the reports from the different laboratories) and could not provide a figure on the number of samplers in Denmark because any harvester can be a sampler. According to the information provided by the DVFA, harvesters organisations tend to use always the same samplers. · Results are not representative of the whole production area as harvesters take samples where they want to harvest and not at designated points. · The protocols for harvesters included in national legislation are not sufficiently detailed. The practices used during sampling and transport of samples affect the quality of samples (see Appendix 1 for further details). · Harvesters cook samples before sending them to laboratories (national legislation indicate that samples are normally heat-treated before analysis, either by the immersion in boiling water for 30 seconds o by steaming). This may lead to an unknown underestimation in the quantity of biotoxins present in the original sample (see paragraphs 44, 45 and 46).

The absence of designated official and private laboratories, and the lack of official supervision and verification of the laboratories, undermines the ability of Danish authority to back up the decision it takes regarding harvesting of molluscs.

The DVFA takes decisions based on results of checks carried out by harvesters, but without taking all necessary steps to ensure their reliability. The heat treatment of most of the samples, the lack of training of samplers, absence of control and supervision of samplers, sampling points not representative of the area, etc. diminish the trustworthiness of these results. This poses a risk that live bivalve molluscs with high levels of E. coli contamination, or with biotoxins and heavy metals content above the regulated limits, might be placed on the market.

The DVFA has a yearly project to verify the reliability of harvesters' results. This project consists of a reduced number of samples (30 per year for biotoxins and toxin- producing plankton; 60 for E. coli 12) that officials take at the same location and moment than harvesters, following the corresponding DVFA sampling protocols. The audit team noted that: · The audit evaluated a case with discrepancies between the two results, with official results higher than operators' results. The DVFA disregarded the results from its official samples and used the harvesters lower results for action or decision (see paragraph 19). This makes the entire verification project of no value. In addition, the DVFA does not carry out an assessment of the discrepant results to check, for example, a correspondence with particular samplers. 12 According to the data provided, harvesters analysed around 950 samples E. coli in 2020, 470 toxin-producing plankton and 670 for biotoxins. 10 · According to the project, officials take five samples for E. coli testing from each production area to mirror the harvesters' sampling (i.e. five samples every time), which reduces the temporal official data available. · Results from official testing for biotoxins show that two or three samples from the same location are often taken, resulting also in a reduction of the temporal official data available.

The DVFA takes the following decisions after harvesters' own-checks results: a) For microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs · The DVFA temporarily downgrades the classification of production areas following results over the expected ones for a given classification. However, permanent A production areas temporarily downgraded to B, go back to A following acceptable results of five samples taken on the same day, which is contrary to Article 52(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 (this reversion should only take place if the evaluation of the results available for the review period determines compliance with the corresponding standards). The DVFA permanently downgrades production areas if 5% of results in the previous three months are above the expected ones, which is also not in line with the same article. · In permanently classified production areas, the DVFA grants a higher or lower classification to smaller zones within the production area, based on the E. coli testing results (i.e. a three nautical miles square with A status within a class B production area), which is contrary to Article 52(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. · The number of dilutions made during the analyses of samples was not enough to provide an exact number when results were >18,000 (see paragraph 11), therefore the DVFA cannot determine if these areas exceeded the limit of 46,000 established in Articles 54(3) and 55(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 for class B and C. Consequently, in these cases, it could not take adequate decisions for reclassification and/or closure of production areas. b) For the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water · National legislation contains a list of toxin-producing plankton species considered as relevant for each of the biotoxin groups in the Danish waters, and establishes "action limits" for each species. These action limits trigger the individual sampling of all the individual production areas within the "algae surveillance area", but harvesting continues if biotoxin testing results are below the regulatory limits. This is contrary to Articles 61(3)(a) and 61(7) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, which require, respectively, an intensive sampling following results suggesting an accumulation of toxins in live bivalve mollusc flesh and the precautionary closures of production areas until results of toxin analysis are obtained. c) For the presence of biotoxins in live bivalve molluscs 11 · As required in Article 62(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the DVFA keeps production areas closed and prevents the harvesting of live bivalve molluscs when biotoxins results exceed the regulatory limits established. recommendations.text: To ensure that marine gastropods harvested from production areas which are not classified are subject to official controls, as required in Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. Recommendation based on conclusion No 35. Associated findings Nos 22, 23 and 24.

citations.text: The only relevant species harvested in Denmark is common whelk (Buccinum undatum). The DVFA does not carry out the official controls required in Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624, in particular aimed at verifying the health standards and the specific requirements set out respectively in Chapters V and IX of Section VII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

According to national legislation, food business operators in establishments have to take samples to analyse E. coli, biotoxins and heavy metals. Based on a document from DTU, the DVFA had decided to reduce the frequency of gastropods sampling. Currently, sampling is limited to three months of the year (from April to June) with one sample in the first fishing week in each production area, and an additional sample every four weeks during that period. However, the document does not provide robust basis for this decision. It intends to find a justification for a continuous sampling instead of presenting a solid risk assessment scientifically justifying the decision to reduce frequencies (the document states that, based on the available scientific basis and data, it is not possible to provide very clear justifications and arguments for continuous sampling for the presence of biotoxins in gastropods in Denmark).

The DVFA has a yearly project to verify the reliability of food business operators' results similar to the one described in paragraph 18. 12 5.1.6 Movement of live bivalve molluscs and registration document accompanying batches

The fact that the DVFA does not carry out official controls on marine gastropods and that it requires from operators a very reduced number of testing, poses the risk that whelks with biotoxins content above the regulated limits might be placed on the market.

responses.response: The DVFA has two sampling projects a year (verification) on ired in non-filtering sea snails. These deal with the control of biotoxins and heavy metals, respectively. Based on the recommendation from SANTE F, the DVFA will look into whether these verification-sampling projects should be adjusted.

Consequently, it does not use the tools that would have allowed it to detect the deficiencies noted by the audit team. 5.2.1 Laboratories for microbiology

The DVFA provided a list of private laboratories with a contract with the DVFA to carry out the analyses of harvesters' own-check samples. Harvesters can decide which of these laboratories to use. The audit team asked to meet with one of these laboratories to assess the testing of the lipophilic toxin group, but the laboratory refused to meet the audit team or to provide information to the DVFA. Therefore, the findings below for the lipophilic toxin group relate exclusively to a documentary revision of the laboratory mentioned in paragraph 41.

Regarding the ASP laboratory reviewed: · The laboratory carries out the qualitative and quantitative analyses using methods alternative to the EU reference ones (apparently due to the request of the competent authority of the Member State where this laboratory is located). The corresponding national accreditation body has accredited both methods. Although the quantitative method can be considered as an international recognised validated method, as required in Annex V, Chapter II(A) to Regulation (EU) 2019/627, this is not the case for the qualitative method (Annex V, Chapter II(B) of the same Regulation). All samples are tested with the qualitative method and only when results are above a certain threshold (1mg of domoic acid per kilogramme) the laboratory uses the quantitative method, which represents around 1% of the tests. · The laboratory validated the qualitative method in 2013, with material different from the certified reference material, and it has not renewed the validation since then. The laboratory did the validation using raw bivalve molluscs' matrix for blue mussel, oyster and cockle. However, testing uses heat-treated samples, which is not the matrix used in the validation of the method, and this may have an impact on the testing results due to the potential matrix effect. · The laboratory validated the quantitative method in 2004 and it has not renewed the validation since then. Recently, in 2020, the laboratory carried out the verification of the use of new equipment for this method. The validation was done using raw bivalve molluscs matrix for blue mussel, oyster and cockle (it is in the process to include tunicates) However, testing uses heat-treated samples, which is not the matrix used in the validation of the method, and this may have an impact on the testing results due to the potential matrix effect. · The participation in the last proficiency testing for the quantitative method shows satisfactory results, despite the fact that the bivalve molluscs species of the test samples were different that the ones validated. However, since for this participation, the laboratory used raw bivalve molluscs (as in the validation) instead of the normal practice that is the testing of heat-treated samples, the proficiency testing results lack reliability for the testing performed.

Regarding the PSP laboratory reviewed: · The laboratory has the EU reference method accredited by the corresponding national accreditation body. However, during the performance of the method, it deviates from it and from the corresponding EURL standard operational procedure in the heat treatment of the sample, which, consequently, may have an impact on the testing results. 17 · The laboratory validated the method in 2012; it has not renewed the validation since then. The validation report stated that it used raw bivalve molluscs' matrix for the validation, but did not provide information on the bivalve mollusc species used for it. · As mentioned before, biotoxin testing is mostly carried out with heat-treated bivalve molluscs, which is not the matrix used in the validation of the method, and this may have an impact on the testing results due to the potential matrix effect. · The laboratory does not test all the relevant PSP compounds (i.e. GTX6 and C3,4 are missing). · The participation results of the last proficiency testing shows good results for total toxicity (sum of all the compounds) in two samples, but an unsatisfactory result of - 5.5 in the third sample. The assessment of results shows that two compounds (i.e. GTX1-4 and dcSXT) are not detected in any of the three samples and two other compounds (i.e. GTX2-3 and STX) are not detected in the third sample. The laboratory suspects of false negatives but did not find conclusive explanation for these results. It did not carry out any further investigation (it stated that this biotoxin is very unusual to find so they did not do any further investigation; in addition, there was no sufficient remaining sample for re-testing). · The lack of testing of certain compounds and the underreporting of other compounds poses a risk of underestimation of PSP if such an episode occurs.

Regarding lipophilic toxin laboratories (findings are limited to the assessment of the laboratory procedures and the last participation in a proficiency testing of the laboratory carrying out the analyses of official and the harvesters' samples since 1 January 2021): · This laboratory procedure is not in line with the last version of the EURL (which is dated in 2015) and it deviates from the EURL procedure in the extraction of the lipophilic toxin compounds. · The laboratory does not detect all the relevant compounds of the lipophilic toxin group. · As mentioned before, biotoxin testing is carried out with heat-treated bivalve molluscs. This deviates from the EU reference method for lipophilic toxins, therefore it may have an impact on the testing results. · The proficiency testing results shows unsatisfactory and questionable results for some of the compounds of this group. The laboratory suspects there is a problem with the procedure of extraction. If it is the case, there is a risk of underestimation of the lipophilic toxin group if such an episode occurs (the lipophilic toxin group is the most common biotoxin in Danish waters). Conclusions on laboratories
The DVFA has access to adequate laboratory capacity, but lacks the oversight of their 18 work; therefore, it cannot assure the proper performance of laboratory testing activities.

citations.text: Two laboratories share the role of National Reference Laboratory (NRL) for E. coli, the DVFA and the DTU laboratories. The DVFA does not consider necessary to designate the DTU as NRL, which is not in line with Article 100(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The DVFA provided to the audit team the service contract that was in place between the DVFA and the DTU for the period 2017-2020, which included the list of tasks to be done. It also provided the list of NRLs (based on repealed EU legislation, Regulation (EC) No 882/2004), indicating the responsibilities of each one6. However, tasks required analysis for the parameters E. coli, biotoxins, and potentially toxic algae. 4 in Article 101(1)(b) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 were not included, and the DVFA confirmed that neither of these laboratories carried them out.

Contrary to Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, there is no NRL for biotoxins in Denmark. The DVFA explained that the DTU laboratory was the NRL until the end of 2020; the new one, the DVFA laboratory, was in the process of setting up the biotoxins methods. 5.1.1 Classification of production areas

The absence of an NRL for biotoxins and the fact that one of the NRLs for E. coli is not designated and that they do not fulfil all their responsibilities and tasks, is an important shortcoming that diminishes the reliability of results in an official system that is based on results from (a number of) private laboratories.

As described in paragraph 8, and contrary to Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, there is no NRL for biotoxins. The NRL's tasks established in Article 101(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are not carried out. Taking into account the results in 16 participation in proficiency testing (described in paragraph 45 and 46 below), the implementation of Article 101(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, regarding the appropriate follow-up of these tests by an NRL is of utmost importance.

The absence of a NRL for biotoxins and the existence of NRLs for E coli, which do not fulfil all the NRL responsibilities and tasks, negatively affect the harmonisation and improvement in the performance of testing methods by other official and private laboratories. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION 19 The official control system in place does not meet the requirements of EU legislation in most of the relevant parts. The classification and monitoring of production areas, and the decisions that the authority takes are inadequate. The absence of oversight over laboratories and the shortcomings in analytical methods, particularly for biotoxins, constitute a serious limitation for the authorities to rely on testing results. The current system does not contain the necessary elements to reliably prevent potential public health risks and thus, live bivalve molluscs contaminated with E. coli and bivalve molluscs with biotoxins exceeding the regulatory limits might reach the market. Except for the availability of sanitary surveys, the situation in Denmark has not improved since the previous audit in 2012. The competent authorities have not implemented adequate actions to address the relevant recommendations of the previous report. 7 CLOSING MEETING During the closing meeting held on 12 May 2021, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit to the competent authority. During this meeting, the competent authority acknowledged the findings and the preliminary conclusions underlining that the aim of the DVFA is to place safe food on the market. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The Danish competent authorities are requested to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. recommendations.text: To ensure that staff performing ABP official controls and other official activities receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently and to perform official controls and other official activities in a consistent manner. Legal basis: Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Recommendation based on conclusion: 16 Associated findings: 9, 37 and 39

citations.text: The audit team obtained evidence of past training courses (since 2019 till 2022, included) provided to the DVFA staff carrying out official controls and noted that, except for rules on handling SRM, none of the training courses provided covered ABP requirements applicable to operators acting along the ABP chain. Moreover, all of the DVFA inspectors met stated that have not ever received a specific ABP training, except for rules on SRM, and they had to self-educate on the ABP rules, what was in their opinion challenging due to complexity of the ABP legislation. The lack of appropriate training on ABP, to enable staff performing official controls to undertake their duties competently and to preform official controls in a consistent manner, is not in line with the requirements of Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

DVFA did not provide, in the last four years, the ABP specific training to the staff verifying ABP requirements along the ABP chain. Moreover, existing operating control procedures, manuals and guides do not provide sufficient instructions to staff to enable them to competently and consistently carry out their inspection duties on operators acting along the chain of ABP and DP. The lack of appropriate support, in terms of training and documented procedures, to the staff performing official controls along the ABP chain undermines the overall quality and effectiveness of these controls.

Official controls in slaughterhouses and meat cutting plants cover ABP requirements with very narrow focus, often omitting or misinterpreting basic requirements for categorisation of ABP (which in turn determines their further destination), their use and disposal. When comparing inspection results recorded in the inspection reports and the operators' routine daily practices in visited meat establishments, the audit team noted that official controls did not notice that certain operators mixed various categories of ABP without downgrading, as required, the resulting ABP to the highest risk category. The controls did not identify the incorrect categorisation of ABP and their subsequent dispatch to destinations that are not authorised under EU rules. For instance, Category 2 (e.g. tissues of animals presenting signs of transmissible diseases or collected from the establishments floors) and Category 1 materials (e.g. ABP containing residues of SRM) were dispatched to biogas plants without prior processing and/or to processing plants approved for processing of Category 3 material (from which derived products can be used for feeding of farmed animals).

The VIUs' inspectors interviewed by the audit team demonstrated a high level of awareness of ABP requirements. However, in the absence of ABP specific control guides, the evidence of the inspections carried out showed that these were neither conducted consistently nor systematically checked the relevant aspects. Consequently, some of the applicable requirements had been checked multiple times and some not at all.

responses.response: r The DVFA will initiate new training programs, which will ensure that proper introduction and training is given to the staff performing official controls on ABP. This is carried out through a more systematic peer-to-peer training and an intro training program, which is developed and approved in a cooperation between the staff in the Head Office and in the local inspection Units. This is expected to be in place by the beginning of 2024.

citations.text: The DVFA has put in place numerous written procedures, manuals, guidelines and checklists supporting the staff during their official control duties, including inspections and sampling. The audit team examined these documents and noted the following: a. The guides, manuals and procedures for general organisation of official controls apply across the food and the feed areas of the DVFA controls and, except for SRM, do not contain specific references or requirements for carrying out ABP controls. b. The guides, manuals, procedures and checklist covering specific areas and types of operators, establishments and plants are entirely food and feed orientated, and refer solely to requirements of the food, the feed, the animal health and the animal welfare legislation. Except for SRM and sampling on DP at APB operators, they cover none of the ABP requirements applicable to operators acting along the ABP chain, even though numerous operators in the country, including these from the food and the feed sector, generate and/or handle ABP and/or DP. 5 Therefore, the documented control procedures are not adequate and sufficiently specific to support the staff performing official controls along the ABP chain and to ensure the effectiveness, appropriateness, quality and consistency of those controls. This is not in line with requirements of Article 5(1)(a) and (b) and Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

DVFA did not provide, in the last four years, the ABP specific training to the staff verifying ABP requirements along the ABP chain. Moreover, existing operating control procedures, manuals and guides do not provide sufficient instructions to staff to enable them to competently and consistently carry out their inspection duties on operators acting along the chain of ABP and DP. The lack of appropriate support, in terms of training and documented procedures, to the staff performing official controls along the ABP chain undermines the overall quality and effectiveness of these controls.

The existing guidelines and manuals for official controls in the meat producing sector (applying country-wide) do not cover ABP requirements, except these related to the removal of SRM (see finding 10).

The audit team analysed existing control guidelines, manuals and instructions and a selection of inspection reports provided by DVFA and noted that: a. Official controls in dairy establishments are feed-orientated and, while focusing on products of milk origin destined for feeding purposes (mostly a whey), do not cover other ABP destined for disposal. Moreover, within a limited selection of requirements applicable to ABP destined for feeding purposes, inspection reports lack information on verification of testing requirements applicable to feed materials 11 of animal origin laid down in Chapter 1 of Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. b. Official controls on operators running kitchen activities and generating catering waste focus on requirements and rules derived from the food hygiene and animal health legislation, omitting requirements of the EU ABP legislation. c. Official controls at farms (carried out by the DVFA and the DAA), cover different requirements; namely: i) these by DVFA are limited to checks on conditions for temporary storing of fallen animals and the time of their collection (requirement derived from the animal health legislation), and ii) those by the DAA cover feed hygiene and feed ban (the requirements derived from the feed and TSE legislation). Neither of the controls cover requirements of ABP legislation applicable to farms (e.g. the conditions for the use of ABP of milk origin by farms depending on the type of ABP they receive, and these applicable to ABP originating at farms either due to on-farm slaughter or for fallen animals, for example: collection, transport, disposal, documentation accompanying ABP consignments, etc.). 5.2.3.2 Official controls in ABP plants

The VIUs' inspectors interviewed by the audit team demonstrated a high level of awareness of ABP requirements. However, in the absence of ABP specific control guides, the evidence of the inspections carried out showed that these were neither conducted consistently nor systematically checked the relevant aspects. Consequently, some of the applicable requirements had been checked multiple times and some not at all.

responses.response: The DVFA will create control supporting guides for the control of ABP, which will ensure consistency and documentation. The guides will be directed to the various situation where control of ABP is done. This is expected to be carried out by the end of 2023.

audits.title: Slaughter hygiene and meat inspection requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that the ante- and post-mortem inspections as well as the health- marking of carcasses are in line with Articles 11(4), 12(3), 17, 19(1)(k), 25, 30(2) 43(1), 43(2), 45(a), (h), (o), (q), (r) and 48(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 and 17(d)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 4 and 77. Associated findings Nos 1, 12, 28, 39-42, 44, 49-52, 55, 57 and 73.

citations.text: The CCA has adopted several legal acts and guidelines, relevant for the scope of this audit, in recent years. According to the CCA, the changes introduced by these are mainly updates to reflect changes made to EU legislation. The CAs and food business operators (FBOs) are implementing the updated legislation and guidance documents. However, · Guidance No 9504/2021 (on meat inspection), contains certain provisions for post- mortem inspection (PMI) in red meat slaughterhouses that are not in line with Regulation (EU) 2019/627 (see paragraphs 49 and 50). · Guideline No 9853/2017 (on microbiological criteria for foodstuffs) contains certain provisions that are not in line with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 (see paragraphs 69 and 70).

The official control system is supported by updated national legislation and guidelines. Certain provisions in the guidance documents are contrary to the requirements of Regulations (EU) 2019/627 and (EC) No 2073/2005 which impacts the application of related EU requirements.

There are cooperation and coordination mechanisms in place within DVFA's departments and a system of notification of other CAs when the non-compliances identified need follow-up by other CAs. The OVs at slaughterhouse level notify welfare and animal identification issues that may concern the transport or farm level. Nonetheless, the outcome of on the farm/database controls is not considered when making decisions on animal identification (see paragraphs 40 and 41). 4 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest

The CA considers that, the recommendation on enforcing provisions that animals are clean prior to slaughter, has been addressed. Nonetheless, the findings at the time of the current audit suggest that the recommendation was not adequately addressed. AMI in cattle did not include checking animal cleanliness (see paragraph 39). This was replaced by CA audits of FBOs' systems for dealing with dirty cattle. 5.2.6 Enforcement

In large slaughterhouses the OVs permanently present during slaughter perform AMI. In the small slaughterhouses, private veterinarians employed on a contract basis for AMI perform this task. AMI includes controls on most of the relevant aspects (e.g. health status, identification, food chain information and animal welfare). However, AMI does not include verification of FBOs compliance with their obligation to ensure that animals have a clean hide, skin or fleece, so as to avoid any unacceptable risk of contamination of the fresh meat during slaughter. This is not in line with Article 11(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Animal health and animal welfare findings of AMI are reported to the relevant services 9 and on-farm investigations are conducted when considered necessary. However, the OVs allow slaughter for human consumption of unidentified or incorrectly identified bovine animals in the absence of an adequate investigation to ascertain the identity of the animal.

When a bovine is presented for slaughter with eartags of an animal that appears as belonging to the category of stolen/dead on large grazing areas (and not found) in the central bovine database or is without eartags, the owner is allowed to make a sworn declaration for a change of details in the central bovine database. The CA allows slaughter for human consumption if the breed, sex and age of the animal matches the (new details) notified by the farmer and accepted by the database. The CA does not receive the outcome of a(possible) investigation before making the decision on the animal. (2)

In the cases assessed, the OVs were aware that red meat animals need to be inspected less than 24 hours after arrival and less than 24 hours before slaughter and had agreed arrangements with the FBOs to ensure this happens, including when animals were delivered during the weekend. AMI of all animals is documented. Nonetheless, should the agreed arrangements for the FBOs (to call the OV for AMI when new animals are presented for slaughter) fail to deliver, there is no reconciliation carried out between the number of animals passing AMI with the number passing PMI, nor are the OVs required to do so.

The CA has put provisions in place for AMI to be carried out at the holding of provenance. This option is used for emergency slaughter of animals and for animals that are difficult to handle. Approximately 350 private veterinarians have been designated as OVs for AMI on farms. The designation was not precluded by training or a system of measures to safeguard potential conflict of interest. The CA organised an information session and plans for more such sessions to be delivered to reach all designated OVs. Ante-mortem inspection - poultry

In the cases assessed there were sufficient OVs/OAs to cover all inspection posts during production and for all carcases to receive PMI. There are arrangements in place for PMI including official controls for Trichinella in pigs, tuberculosis and cysticercosis in bovines and pigs. The "in principle" standard are Articles 18-24 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, while in certain circumstances (e.g. for outdoor pigs) the inspection maintains the additional incisions and palpations as per previous Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Nonetheless, certain provisions of Guidance 9504/2021 differ from the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 · The guidance allows carcases with certain pathology and contamination, including abscess and pus contamination, to pass PMI. The FBO is required to remove such PMI findings (that are considered as not severe by the CA) and health-mark the carcasses. The CA carries out controls on a limited number of carcases and a zero tolerance system is not in place. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 45 (o) and (r) and 48 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. · The guidance allows carcases of bovine animals more than 2 years old, where less than 10 Cysticercus cysts are found at PMI, to be passed as fit for consumption, without freezing, after removal of body parts where the cysts were found. In the bovine slaughterhouse visited, the limit was lowered to 5 cysts, but the carcases were still passed as fit for human consumption, without freezing, contrary to the 11 requirements of Articles 30 and 45(h) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

In addition, PMI does not check for the presence/safe removal of SRM, contrary to the requirements of Article 17(d)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Carcases with SRM are health-marked, contrary to the requirements of Article 45(q) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The OVs do not subsequently check if the FBO has removed SRM from all health-marked carcases either. The OVs check FBOs' procedures for SRM removal, during audits on related FBOs procedures, a few times a year.

The cows' udders were not inspected unless they went for human consumption and/or pet food in the case assessed. The OV explained this is in line with the clarification received from central level. However, this approach is contrary to the requirements of Article 19(1)(k) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

The audit team identified different additional gaps in PMI in the sheep and bovine slaughterhouses visited, contrary to the requirements of Articles 12(3), 17 and 45(r) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627: · In the large bovine slaughterhouse, the inadequate presentation of the spleen by the FBO (long highlighted by the OV, but not addressed) resulted in the spleen not being routinely inspected;. · In the small slaughterhouses, several gaps in PMI had been noted by the audit team, but not by the supervisor present that day [e.g. in the sheep slaughterhouse, the OV was not checking the lower part of the carcase (and therefore missing several carcases with contamination in the lower part), not palpating the lungs and livers, inspecting green offal only at random; for bovine carcases the OV could not inspect the upper part of the carcase (as was not using a stand); the kidneys were not presented decapsulated neither for sheep nor for cattle and were not adequately inspected]; · The OVs performing PMI had stamped carcases with some "minor" (in terms of size) contamination in both small slaughterhouses and to a larger extent in the sheep slaughterhouse. The supervising OV identified only a small number thereof.

The CA has arrangements in place for poultry PMI to be carried out by OVs and OAs as well as in some cases by authorised slaughterhouse staff under the supervision of the OV. The slaughterhouse staff is authorised to perform certain PMI tasks only after undergoing relevant training and passing an assessment by the CA. The arrangements for poultry PMI were found to be largely satisfactory in the case assessed, where slaughterhouse staff were performing PMI, apart from the absence of a system for the OV/OA to check viscera and body cavities on a representative sample for each flock, contrary to the requirements of Article 25 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 5.3.2 Official controls over food business operators' obligations Food Chain Information and animal identification Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 in conjunction with its Annex II, Section III and Article 9 and 10, 40, 41 42 and 43.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

The OVs check FBO procedures to ensure that only animals/batches of animals that are properly identified and traceable to origin are slaughtered and these checks have been satisfactory in the cases assessed, with FBOs bringing inadequately identified and unidentified animals to the attention of the OVs. Nonetheless, the action taken by the CA in these cases is not fully satisfactory (see paragraphs 40 and 41). General and specific hygiene requirements, including HACCP based procedures Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and Article 46 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 13 Findings

Health-marking is applied either by the OV or by the FBO under the supervision of the OV. In the case assessed, the health mark was kept under official control outside of working hours. Controls on the application of identification marks are included in the audit plan and are carried out at least once a year. However, contrary to the requirements of Article 48(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the health mark is also applied in certain cases when there are grounds for declaring the meat unfit for human consumption (see paragraphs 49-52).

There is a system in place for meat inspection on bovine, ovine, porcine and poultry that covers most relevant aspects. However, the effectiveness of AMI and, to a larger extent, PMI is impacted by a number of systemic shortcomings. 5.4 RAPID ALERT SYSTEM FOR FOOD AND FEED (RASFF) Legal requirements Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715 (IMSOC Regulation). citations.text: The CA provides training to the official control staff, including OVs and official auxiliaries (OAs). In the absence of a national system to deliver OV training in line with Article 13 and Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2019/624, the supervisors assess the training needs upon recruitment of an OV and deliver the training considered needed. The CA highlighted that a centrally developed/harmonised training is in the process of being developed. The training needs for OVs already active are identified during routine supervision and then custom made for the respective OV, sometimes also delivered by the supervisor. When the supervisor is not able to adequately detect knowledge gaps and poor performance ­ as seen during the audit for small slaughterhouses ­ the OV does not receive the adequate training.

The training topics for a new OV (developed by one of the four supervisors of OVs in small slaughterhouses) did not cover aspects on which the OV is required to perform controls such as animal welfare and animal identification. In addition, no control procedure is available for the latter. The OV performing AMI, PMI and some animal welfare controls in one of the small slaughterhouses visited did not have a satisfactory knowledge of PMI requirements (see paragraph 52) and of certain animal welfare 5 requirements (e.g. 0.7- 0.8A for 15 seconds was considered better than the 1A for effective electric stun).

The OVs benefit from the technical support of the supervisors. The supervisors for the teams in large slaughterhouse met by the audit team were knowledgeable in the areas under review. Nonetheless, the audit team identified gaps in the knowledge of the supervisor for small slaughterhouses, met during the audit (e.g. as regards prevention of cross-contamination and PMI ­ see paragraphs 52, 60-62, 64). The supervisor also had an incorrect understanding of certain animal welfare requirements (e.g. considering captive bolt a stun-to-kill method for which effectiveness of stunning did not need to be checked).

As the supervisor is the only CA member of staff performing controls on FBOs' hygiene requirements, as well as supervision of OVs contracted for AMI, PMI and some animal welfare controls, these knowledge gaps have impacted the effectiveness of the controls in the small establishments visited during the current audit (see paragraphs 60-62, 64, 66). The same supervisor was in charge of controls in 25 small slaughterhouses, assessing the training needs, training and supervising the contracted OVs in these establishments. This questions the effectiveness of the controls in the remaining small slaughterhouses.

The CA structure, organisation and resources, including support, are adequate, overall, to deliver effective controls in large slaughterhouses. However, this is not the case for small slaughterhouses, where the system relies heavily on a small number of staff to perform audits, act as supervisors, determine training needs and deliver the training of OVs. This system has proved inadequate in terms of detecting poor hygiene practices as well as poor staff performance/knowledge gaps and has resulted in ineffective controls.

recommendations.text: To update the contingency plan and the epidemiological inquiries to be used in the investigation of aquatic diseases, in accordance with the rules laid down in Regulation (EU) 2016/429. 26 · Article 5(1)(i) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. · Article 43 and 57 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. · Articles 4 and 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Based on conclusion 20 and associated finding 7.

citations.text: The competent authority has a contingency plan on how to contain and manage outbreaks of listed or emerging Category A diseases in aquaculture animals. The contingency plan is available on the intranet of the DVFA. However, the last version of the contingency plan is dated 2010 and the DVFA is planning to update it in 2024, together with a new format for the epidemiological inquiry that the Team Aqua has to use to investigate aquatic diseases.

The competent authorities need to update the contingency plan, together with the epidemiological inquiry to be used for the investigation of aquatic diseases, taking into account the new provisions set by the AHL. This would allow the competent authorities to act, in line with the EU legislation, if a Category A disease is occurring in the country.

responses.response: al Being prepared is an important precautionary principle to enable a rapid and effective iseases, response to any outbreak of a notifiable disease. Due to the resent development of EU) food and veterinary crises in Europe, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration (DVFA) has an increased focus on contingency planning throughout the organization. As a result, a contingency policy and a general contingency plan have been developed for the entire organization. The DVFA is currently in the process of updating and developing new contingency plans for category A diseases. The Danish contingency plan for category A diseases consists of a general plan ("partial plan" in attachment 1) and relevant action plans in relation to e.g. culling, disposal, cleaning and disinfection, and supplemented by disease specific action cards and templates (see attachment 1). The Veterinary partial plan regarding category A diseases includes category A diseases of aquatic animals. The plan is based on AHL and is expected to be completed in the 3rd quarter of 2024.

recommendations.text: To align and to verify the procedures for the risk assessment of the approved aquaculture establishments, on the basis of the provisions of the EU legislation, taking account all relevant risk parameters. · Article 6(1) and Part 1, Annex II of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/691. · Part I of Annex VI to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689. Based on conclusion 41 and associated findings 36, 37 and 53.

citations.text: The audit team visited one trout establishment approved and ranked as medium risk by the Team Aqua, since aquatic animals are sent to put and take lakes only. However, the competent authority didn't consider the high risk of infection due to the close proximity to an angling lake next to it, the recurrence of the IHN infection with two outbreaks occurred respectively in 2021 and 2022 and the high number of movements in and out the establishment. This is not in line with Chapter 2 a) and b), Part I of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2020/689, as regards the risk ranking to be applied in certain approved aquaculture establishments in this regard.

The audit team visited another trout establishment approved and ranked as medium risk, which has been infected with IHN in September 2022. Fish is kept for approximately three months, from 200 to 500 grams. The operator is consigning to more than 50 establishments, of which approximately 70 % are put and take lakes, and it is receiving from other 20 establishments. Nevertheless, the competent authority didn't consider the high risk of infection due to the high number of movements going in and out the establishment. This is not in line with Regulation (EU) 2020/689, as mentioned in the previous finding. The competent authority agreed with the audit team on the need to review the risk assessment for ranking approved establishments, together with the DTU Aqua.

The competent authority have implemented effectively the new process of registration and approval of the aquaculture establishments, according to the AHL, with clear guidelines and instructions for the correct implementation from the VIU. However, in some cases the Team Aqua has assessed the risk of the approved establishments not taking into account all the criteria listed in Annex VI to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689. This may increase the risk of not detecting the IHN during the regular health visits carried out by the Team Aqua.

The official veterinarians of the Team Aqua are implementing, in particular, the risk-based health surveillance in all approved aquaculture establishments, as foreseen by Chapter 1, Part III, Annex VI of Regulation (EU) 2020/689. The frequency of the health visits and possible sampling depends on the risk of the approved aquaculture establishment, determined by the DVFA as high, medium or low. However, the DVFA ranked some of the establishments visited by the audit team, as explained in previous findings 36 and 37, with a risk ranking (i.e. "medium" instead of "high) which is resulting in a frequency of health visits too low.

responses.response: Between November 2023 and March 2024, the DVFA and DTU-Aqua have on developed a new model for the risk assessment of approved aquaculture establishments (see attachment 2). The risk ranking is done for each category C ion disease, and summarised in an overall risk for the assessed establishment. All risk factors listed in EU legislation has been considered in connection with the risk ranking for each disease, and if considered relevant they are included in the risk ranking. 38 The proposed action is therefore already completed. In connection with the next risk-based health visits, the VIU will reassess the risk ranking of each approved aquaculture establishment in accordance with the new model. The result of the risk ranking will be included in the control report for each control visit. Page: 1 ort, received 10 March 2024 e recommendations of report ref. recommendations.text: To approve the cleaning and disinfection procedures applied in all the water exchange points, in order to ensure the conditions required by the EU legislation. · Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2020/990. · Article 192 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 Based on conclusion 111 and associated finding 107.

citations.text: The competent authorities in Finland notified an IHN outbreak in June 2022, following a consignment of aquatic animals received from Denmark. The DVFA traced and tested, with negative results, the two establishments delivering respectively eggs and fishes to the confirmed outbreak in Finland, explaining to the audit team that a possible transmission of the disease was 24 due to the transit through one of the two water exchange points registered in Denmark. As a consequence, the DVFA established a specific procedure for the cleaning and disinfection of one of the two water exchange points, with all transporters requested to transit that specific water exchange point when delivering fish for intra-EU trade to other free IHN compartments. However, no specific procedures for the cleaning and disinfection have been approved for the other water exchange point registered in Denmark. 5.5.3 Certification

The competent authorities implemented the certification for the trade of aquatic animals from Denmark to other Member States as required by EU legislation. However, the competent authority deemed transportation of aquatic animals, transiting through a water exchange point in Denmark without proper disinfection procedures, as the possible cause of the transmission of IHN to another Member State This is not in line with the EU legislation, that requires that the competent authorities must certify that animals are not transported under conditions that jeopardize their health status.

responses.response: As described in finding 107, only two water exchange points are registered in ensure Denmark, and the DVFA has approved the cleaning and disinfection procedures of one of the two water exchange points. The DVFA has informed the operator, as well as the transporters and aquaculture industry organisation, that the other water exchange point cannot be used in connection with any transport of fish before the cleaning and disinfection procedures of this water exchange point have been approved by the DVFA. The proposed action is therefore already completed.

recommendations.text: To carry out the regular risk based official controls on transporters and water exchange points, as foreseen by Regulation (EU) 2017/625. · Article 9, 10 and 20 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. · Articles 3 and 4 of Regulation (EU) 2020/990. · Articles 191 to 192 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 Based on conclusion 112 and associated finding 105.

citations.text: The VIUs are carrying out spot-checks of transporters according to Regulation (EU) 1/2005, for animal welfare. However, they are not carrying out the official controls of the transporters registered in the Country. This is not in line with the provisions of paragraph 1 of Articles 9, 10 and 20 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (Official Controls Regulation - OCR), regarding the regular risk based official controls on all operators, including transporters, at any stage of production, processing and distribution of animals, products of animal origin and germinal products. Those official controls would need to address, as well, the activities under the control of operators, i.e., the general obligation on operators as regards biosecurity requirements for the transport of aquatic animals, foreseen by Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2020/990.

The competent authorities have approved the procedures for the cleaning and disinfection of the transporters, one water exchange point, and for all the other documents foreseen by the EU legislation. However, they are not applying regular official controls on transporters and water exchange points, on a risk basis, to verify compliance with the approved procedures and the activities under the control of operators. This is not in line with the EU legislation, and it is not assuring the absence of risk of transmission of IHN or other aquatic diseases with the 25 movement of aquatic animals. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authorities have established a system with effective coordination and verification, clear instructions, and properly trained personnel. The official laboratory network is effective, with high technical standards providing reliable support for disease surveillance. However, some challenges were identified, namely: · Preparedness: the contingency plan being not updated with the new provisions set by the EU legislation may not allow the competent authorities to respond with the measures in line with the EU requirements, in case of an aquatic Category A disease occurring in the Country. · Inconsistent approaches: the risk assessment applied in the approved establishments, not always taking into account all the criteria set by the AH (e.g. frequent movements), poses the risk of IHN not being detected during the health visits carried out, as the annual frequency in some establishments may be too low for their risk level. · Disease control: while the competent authorities notify suspect cases timely and they contain the outbreaks effectively, the absence of an eradication programme for IHN applied at a national level may lead to increased risk of the disease spreading and it reduces the possibility to quickly re-gain the free status in the whole Country. · Legislative alignment: the competent authorities need to approve the cleaning and disinfection protocols for all the water exchange points approved in Denmark and they need to carry out the regular risk based official controls on transporters and water exchange points. 7. At this meeting, the audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. The competent authorities did not indicate any major disagreement with the findings and preliminary conclusions. 8. recommendations.text: The competent authorities should provide effective training and technical support (including specific checklists and work instructions regarding identi- fication and handling of non-compliances), to ensure effective and appropri- ate official controls, including microbiological risks, as required by Article 5(1)(e)(f) and 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.
