citations.text: Regarding DAA, for many years the official controls on fruit and vegetables throughout Denmark have been carried out by the same team of two inspectors (30 official inspec- tions/year). The two inspectors informed the audit team that they had not received any specific training on official controls at primary production relating to microbiological risks.

Employees are introduced to relevant legislation and educated in practical skills and aca- demic subjects to the extent required. Some inspectors participate in other relevant courses outside DVFA such as Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF). However, there was no evidence of any cascade course activity in order to share experiences and knowledge from BTSF courses with other colleagues.

During official inspections observed by the audit team, both DAA and DVFA inspectors and their supervisors demonstrated clear deficiencies in identifying non-compliances. Only when the audit team highlighted evidence of several very critical deficiencies over- looked during official inspections (e.g. cross-contamination and staff misconduct) did inspectors and supervisors acknowledge that these deficiencies represent a real risk for food safety (see paragraphs 19, 20, 35, 48, 49, 52, 57, 65, 66 and 67). Audit / Supervision

However, to date, supervisors were unable to identify and guide inspectors in assessing key deficiencies related to microbiological risks, including those that could lead to direct contamination of food products. Furthermore, the audit team identified that non- conformities are evaluated differently by DVFA inspectors.

A training system has been implemented. However, to date, inspectors and supervisors are unable to assess key deficiencies related to microbiological risks, highlighting a lack of knowledge and experience which, combined with inconsistency in the implementation and enforcement of EU legislation, has a negative impact on the implementation of offi- 5 cial controls.

There is a supervisory system in place for official controls. However, the system fails to identify and correct all shortcomings in official controls. Importers that are importing and distributing risky produce

DVFA informed the audit team that official inspections are carried out in accordance with written procedures and instructions that include the requirement of Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. However, there are no official written procedures regarding the classification, management and evaluation of non-conformities detected during offi- cial inspections and there are no instructions on the actions that inspectors must take to- wards the product when cases of direct contamination of foods are found during an offi- cial inspection.
In addition, in case of reported non-compliances, CAs do not require the FBO to provide an action plan.

Inspectors confirmed to the audit team that there are no specific procedures regarding classification/management of non-compliances including an absence of instructions on the actions to be taken when cases of potential direct contamination of food are found during an official inspection. 5.3.3 Implementation of official controls Legal requirements Articles 9(1)(d), 14 and 44(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; Articles 4 to 8 and Annexes I and II of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004; Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002; Article 3 of Regulation (EU) No 208/2013; Regulation (EU) 2020/2235; Article 1 and Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings Primary production

Presence of birds inside greenhouses and food handling areas, inconsistent use of gloves by harvesting personnel, potential cross-contamination of harvested strawberries either by placing crates directly on the ground or by unhygienic worker practices, excessive presence of cobwebs in all packaging/storage areas of a primary FBO, were not identi- fied as non-compliance by either the inspectors or their supervisor.

There was no evidence that the above-mentioned non-compliances had ever been identi- fied and registered in previous inspections, including during the annual screening on "marketing standards" (see paragraph 38). In addition, the review of previous inspection reports detected very few non-compliances which gives the impression of compliance throughout the country, when this was not the case.

DVFA informed the audit team that their procedures provide inspectors with the power to require corrective action to be taken. However, during the audit, neither the FBOs, nor the inspectors, nor the supervisor took/requested immediate action to segregate potential- ly contaminated products observed by the audit team. Sprout-producing establishment

The inspectors correctly assessed the certification requirements for mung beans imported from a specific third country as seeds for sprouting but neither the inspectors nor the su- pervisor identify that the FBO also sprout imported seeds from other third countries. Therefore, the requirements (e.g. health certificates) for other seeds imported from other third countries have never been verified meaning, DVFA has never fully enforced this requirement.

However, other major non-compliances such as other areas of the establishment where condensation water was dropping on the food, a worker touching dirty surfaces and then product without changing gloves and rust/oil on two electric motors above the produc- tion line were overlooked by inspectors and their supervisor. In the last three years (six official inspections) there was no evidence that the inspectors or supervisor had detected or recorded similar non-compliances requiring correction.

During the debriefing with the FBO the inspectors, with the agreement of the supervisor, concluded that the official report will contain a minor non-conformity related to rusty pipes. Non-conformities regarding direct contamination of the product, even when de- tected by inspectors (condensation falling on the product), were not planned to be docu- mented in the official report. Processors (cut fruits and vegetables)

The audit team observed inspections being carried out at the high care areas (cutting, slicing, chopping area). In one case, even though several non-compliances were detected and recorded by the inspectors, condensation issues (even over the exposed foodstuff), rust and dirt on the ceiling and flaking paint on some equipment was overlooked.

When guided by the audit team, the inspectors identified inadequate cleaning of machin- ery, which the FBO considered as clean and ready to be used. However, there was no ev- idence (official reports) that similar non-compliances had ever been identified in previ- ous inspections as in other processors of FNAO.

The inspectors and the supervisor confirmed to the audit team that, during inspection, non-compliances, like the one observed by the audit team during these official inspec- tions, are usually communicated orally to the FBOs rather than documented in the offi- cial reports.
CAs did not keep the approval of sprout-producing establishments under review when carrying out official controls, contrary to the requirements of Article 148(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 12

Regarding farms, sprout-production establishments and processors, non-compliances are rarely detected and even when detected their severity is underestimated and rarely record- ed. In addition, in case of on-the-spot detected risks, no immediate action is taken on the affected product. This calls into question both the ability of the inspectors to evaluate the non-conformities in a consistent manner and the effectiveness of their supervision. Con- sequently, the deficiencies in the enforcement measures undermines the effectiveness of the system of official controls.

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should implement procedures to ensure the effec- tiveness and appropriateness of official controls, ensuring that inspection reports provide evidence of both adequacy and quality of those controls, in accordance with Articles 5(1) and 13 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusions: 23, 72, 74 and 75. Associated findings: 12, 19, 50 and 67.

citations.text: During official inspections observed by the audit team, both DAA and DVFA inspectors and their supervisors demonstrated clear deficiencies in identifying non-compliances. Only when the audit team highlighted evidence of several very critical deficiencies over- looked during official inspections (e.g. cross-contamination and staff misconduct) did inspectors and supervisors acknowledge that these deficiencies represent a real risk for food safety (see paragraphs 19, 20, 35, 48, 49, 52, 57, 65, 66 and 67). Audit / Supervision

However, to date, supervisors were unable to identify and guide inspectors in assessing key deficiencies related to microbiological risks, including those that could lead to direct contamination of food products. Furthermore, the audit team identified that non- conformities are evaluated differently by DVFA inspectors.

There is a supervisory system in place for official controls. However, the system fails to identify and correct all shortcomings in official controls. This highlights deficiencies in both the knowledge and experience of CAs and subsequent consistency and effective- ness of the implementation and enforcement of EU legislation. 5.3 Official controls 5.3.1 Registration and approval of food business operators Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004; Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013; Articles 10(2), 138(1), 138(2)(c)-(j), 138(3), 138(4) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings Registration

DVFA informed the audit team that their procedures provide inspectors with the power to require corrective action to be taken. However, during the audit, neither the FBOs, nor the inspectors, nor the supervisor took/requested immediate action to segregate potential- ly contaminated products observed by the audit team. Sprout-producing establishment

The inspectors and the supervisor confirmed to the audit team that, during inspection, non-compliances, like the one observed by the audit team during these official inspec- tions, are usually communicated orally to the FBOs rather than documented in the offi- cial reports.
CAs did not keep the approval of sprout-producing establishments under review when carrying out official controls, contrary to the requirements of Article 148(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 12

Regarding farms, sprout-production establishments and processors, non-compliances are rarely detected and even when detected their severity is underestimated and rarely record- ed. In addition, in case of on-the-spot detected risks, no immediate action is taken on the affected product. This calls into question both the ability of the inspectors to evaluate the non-conformities in a consistent manner and the effectiveness of their supervision. Con- sequently, the deficiencies in the enforcement measures undermines the effectiveness of the system of official controls.

Although sprout-producing establishments are identified by DVFA as representing higher risk, the fact that verification of compliance with Regulation (EC) No 208/2013 on certi- fication requirements of imported seeds for sprouting has been overlooked during official controls, in conjunction with the fact that Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 on preliminary tests for seeds and analyses of sprouts has been misinterpreted by the CAs, undermines the effectiveness of such official controls. 5.4 Official sampling procedures Legal Requirements Articles 34 and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; Annex I, Chapter 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. audits.title: evaluate the implementation of official controls on feed hygiene

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently check that feed business operators implement and maintain effective procedures based on hazard analysis and criti- cal control point principles. Legal basis: Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 31. Associated findings: 22 and 23.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 31. Associated findings: 22 and 23.

citations.text: In two compound feed manufacturers visited, the audit team reviewed the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. In one establishment, the hazard identification section of the operators' HACCP plan and the HACCP principles on the critical control point were correct. The audit team could identify some minor shortcomings, and during the audit interview the feed inspector correctly assessed these shortcomings. In the other establishment, the hazard identification section of the operators' HACCP plan was very generic. Several hazards were grouped and assessed together, although the severity and the probability of these hazards were very different (for example several different types of cereals and relevant hazards were assessed as a single group). The operator's monitoring procedure described in its own HACCP system did not reflect the procedure implemented by the operator. The above shortcomings in the implementation of Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) 183/2005 identified by the audit team were overlooked during previous official inspections.

In the two food establishments manufacturing and suppling a by-product to the feed chain, the feed part of operators' HACCP systems were deficient. HACCP documents did not consider any production steps relating to feed production or the procedures for the collection and storage of retained samples. These are not in line with the requirements of Article 7(1) and point 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. HACCP documents did not contain descriptions of the requirements for labelling of feed materials manufactured and several of these requirements were not communicated to the buyers (feed material, compulsory declarations) which is not in line with the requirements of Articles 15 and 16 of Regulations (EC) 767/2009. These deficiencies were not identified in previous inspection reports.

While the planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and official inspections are carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with an appropriate frequency, the effectiveness of these controls is weakened by some shortcomings in the inspectors assessments of (i) feed business operators' hazard analyses and critical control point plans, and (ii) operators' tests on minimisation of cross contamination and on production of suitably homogeneous mixture of feed. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently verify that feed business operators meet the requirements for appropriate checks of the effectiveness of measures they have taken to minimise cross-contamination and produce suitable homoge- nous mixture of feed. Legal basis: point 3 of the section "Production" and points 2 and 3 of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 31. Associated findings: 24 and 25.
recommendations.legal_basis: point 3 of the section "Production" and points 2 and 3 of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 31. Associated findings: 24 and 25.

citations.text: Verification of establishments' tests on homogeneity of mixing (required by point 3 of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005) is included in the scope of the inspections, when applicable. In three compound feed manufacturers visited, the audit team reviewed the operators' documentation on the related homogeneity testing and interviewed the inspectors who usually control those establishments. In one establishment visited, several results of mixing homogeneity tests were unacceptable in the previous 9 months, but the FeBO did not implement any corrective actions. In another establishment, the number of the samples collected was lower than necessary to implement an adequate test. The feed inspectors met indicated 7 that they had experienced difficulties in comprehensively assessing the procedures and the results of the mixing homogeneity tests.

Verification of establishments' tests to assess the measures taken to minimise cross- contamination, required by point 2 of section "Facilities and equipment" and point 3 of section "Production" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, forms part of the inspections, when applicable. In one establishment visited, the analytical results of the testing laboratory were higher than the maximum limit described in Section VII, Annex I to Directive 2002/32 in the last 3 years. However, the FeBO did not implement any corrective actions. In two establishments FeBOs collected only one sample from the first mix after cleaning (flushing) for testing of cross-contamination. In one establishment, several samples were collected from the first mix after flushing, however these samples were pooled and sent to the laboratory as one sample. Similarly, as for verification of operators test on homogeneity of mixing, the feed inspectors met indicated that they had experienced difficulties in comprehensively assessing the procedures and the results of the cross-contamination tests.

While the planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and official inspections are carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with an appropriate frequency, the effectiveness of these controls is weakened by some shortcomings in the inspectors assessments of (i) feed business operators' hazard analyses and critical control point plans, and (ii) operators' tests on minimisation of cross contamination and on production of suitably homogeneous mixture of feed. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that, in the event of established non-compliance(s) being identified, the central competent authority puts arrangements in place to ensure the quality and consistency of the actions taken by its local inspectors in respect of verifica- tion of remediation of the non-compliance(s) by the feed business operator and prevention of further recurrences. Legal basis: Articles 5(1)(b), 13(2) and 138(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion: 56. Associated findings: 53, 54 and 55.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 5(1)(b), 13(2) and 138(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion: 56. Associated findings: 53, 54 and 55.

citations.text: The audit team reviewed the records on seven sampling and one inspection-related non-compliances. The feed inspectors could provide the official reports on the follow- up of these non-compliances. In three cases, these reports provided sufficient information indicating that the FeBOs had carried out investigations to address the deficiency, and/or identify the root cause, and/or prevent the reoccurrence of the identified non-compliances. This is in line with the requirements of Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. However, in four of the sampling-related cases, the competent authority could not provide evidence that the FeBOs carried out adequate investigations to identify the root cause and took actions to prevent the reoccurrence of the identified non-compliances (e.g. evidence on the destruction of contaminated feeds, correction of recipes/labels, modification of HACCP procedures) which is not in line with the above-mentioned legislative requirements.

The inspection related non-compliance arose from a problem with the operator's traceability system. The feed inspector identified this problem in July 2024 and issued a warning to the operator. The feed inspector carried out an on-the-spot follow up inspection at the end of September 2024. The problem still remained during the follow-up inspection. The feed inspector prepared the second warning to the operator and took steps to inform the police. At the time of the audit the second warning was still under legislative check by the relevant unit of the DVFA. The competent authority could not provide evidence that the FeBO took actions to correct the traceability problem and carried out an investigation to prevent the reoccurrence of the problem in its traceability system. The competent authority did not impose any other sanctions (e.g. restrict and/or prohibit the placing on the market of products) relating to the untraceable products. The approach taken by the competent authority is not in line with the requirements of Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Feed inspectors stated that they do not have the right to request action plans with deadlines from FeBOs relating to identified non-compliances. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 13 (1)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusion on the actions taken on non-compliances

Notwithstanding the fact that the competent authority took actions when non- compliances were identified in the course of official controls, the competent authority did not ensure the quality and consistency of official controls in relation to (i) the determination of the origin and extent of the non-compliances, (ii) operator remediation of the non-compliance, and (iii) prevention of further occurrences. Collectively these shortcomings weaken the effectiveness of the system of official controls on feed. 13 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION In Denmark, the planning of official controls on feed is risk-based and is underpinned by the provision of mostly appropriate guidance and operating procedures by the central competent authority, regular training of feed inspectors and the use of duly designated and accredited laboratories. However, the effectiveness of the control system is weakened by several aspects. These include deficient assessment by feed and food inspectors of op- erators' HACCP-plans. The audit team also noted shortcomings relating to the official assessment of operators' testing procedures to demonstrate the effectiveness of measures (i) to minimise cross-contamination arising from the carry-over of coccidiostats and (ii) to manufacture suitable homogeneous mixtures of feed. Feed inspectors carry out follow up inspections on a regular basis, however the competent authorities did not ensure the quality and consistency of these in relation to (i) the determination of the origin and ex- tent of the non-compliances, (ii) operator remediation of the non-compliance, and (iii) prevention of further occurrences. Cumulatively, these shortcomings weaken the effec- tiveness of an otherwise well-functioning system. 7. CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 17 December 2024 with representatives of the DVFA. The audit team presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. The competent authority did not express any disagreement with those. 14 8. RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authority is requested to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below. With regard to those non-compliances noted in the audit report which did not result in a recommendation being made, the competent authority is, nevertheless, requested to address these. The effectiveness of the actions taken to address such non-compliances will be assessed in future audits on this topic. audits.title: evaluate the system of official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union and verification of compliance of border control posts with European Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that any consignments of animals or goods entering the Union that do not comply with the rules referred to in Article 1(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are placed under official detention, the Common Health Entry Docu- ment is finalised and that the operator responsible for the consignment is ordered without delay, to take one of the specified measures, the application of which is supervised. Legal requirements: Articles 55(1), 56(5), 66(1) and 66(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Recommendation based on conclusion No. 48 Associated finding No. 36, 44, 45 and 46

citations.text: As noted in section 5.1.4 above, there are no documented procedures for performing of- ficial checks on consignments of animals entering the EU. A local work instruction has been issued by the BCP Copenhagen airport, which does provide guidance for perform- ing such checks, quarantine and where necessary, euthanasia of consignments of live fish. The audit team noted based on their evaluation of the CHEDs for two consignments of live fish that had been rejected, that the fish were euthanised by the operators respon- sible for the consignments, in both cases using methods of euthanasia that were not in line with the local work instruction at the BCP, and not under supervision by the DVFA. 5.2.4.2 Checks on consignments of goods of animal origin

The audit team noted however, that in cases where non-compliances with the rules in Ar- ticle 1(2) of the OCR were identified, the DVFA had not systematically finalised the CHED, as soon as the official checks including any sampling, had been completed, and a decision that the consignment was not in compliance had been made, which is not in line with Articles 55(1) or 56(5) of the OCR. The audit team also noted that the consign- ments were not systematically placed under official detention as required by Article 66 (1) of the OCR.

Nine of the CHEDs selected and evaluated by the audit team concerned non-compliant consignments. The team noted that the lack of official detention had enabled four of the consignments concerned to be exported or destroyed by the operator without the knowledge or supervision of the DVFA, and prior to the decision being recorded in the CHED.

The DVFA informed the audit team that the operator responsible for a non-compliant consignment is invited to specify which of the measures provided in Article 66(3) of the 11 OCR, would be taken. The DVFA confirmed that, commonly, no deadline for a response is specified for the response and therefore non-compliant goods may remain at the BCP for extended periods of time, which is not in line with the same Article of the OCR. Conclusions on the implementation of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU

However, the significant shortcomings in the decision-making process and follow-up of measures to be taken in the case of non-compliant consignments of animals and goods have the potential to undermine the overall effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the EU. 5.3 COMPLIANCE OF BORDER CONTROL POSTS WITH MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS At the time of the audit, there were 12 BCPs and 14 control points in Denmark included in the lists published on the Commission webpages (5). The audit team carried out on-the-spot visits to three of those BCPs and two control points, detailed in the following table, to verify their compliance with the applicable minimum requirements for BCPs and control points. recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are performed in accordance with documented procedures, and that they are updated as appropriate where control verification procedures identify shortcomings and cover the subject areas for control proce- dures set out in the Official Controls Regulation. Legal requirements: Articles 12(1) and 12(3) and Chapter II of Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Recommendation based on conclusion No. 24 Associated findings No. 7, 8 and 21

citations.text: The DVFA has issued documented procedures in the form of a manual, for the perfor- mance of official controls on goods of animal origin entering the EU. The DVFA in- formed the audit team that there are no documented procedures for the official controls on animals entering the EU, other than a locally issued work instruction at the BCP Co- penhagen airport, and no specific documented procedures for the implementation of measures in case of suspicion of non-compliance, confirmed non-compliance or risk, re- ferred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR.

The audit team noted therefore, that the documented procedures do not include all of the subject areas set out in Chapter II of Annex II to the OCR, which is not in line with Arti- cle 12(1) of that regulation. The audit team found related shortcomings in the implemen- tation of measures in case of non-compliance, as detailed in section 5.2.5 (findings 36 and 44 to 46) below.

The audit team noted that the outcome of the control verifications may be discussed within experience exchange groups held between BCPs and the central International Trade Division which is responsible for documented procedures. However, they are not systematically shared with that Division, which thereby risks compromising the review of documented procedures required by Article 12(3) of the OCR.

However, shortcomings in the documented procedures and in the access to information necessary for the competent authority to confirm that consignments subject to mandatory control at BCPs had been correctly notified undermine the overall effectiveness of the organisation of the official controls. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU The audit team evaluated the implementation of official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Denmark against the applicable EU requirements detailed in Annex 2 to this report, based on an initial selection by the audit team and competent authorities of 39 valid CHEDs recorded in TRACES-NT, and further evidence obtained during the audit, including the on-the-spot visits to three BCPs and two control points. 5.2.1 Prior notification of arrival of consignments

recommendations.text: To ensure that border control posts and control points comply with the minimum requirements for the categories of goods for which they are designated and are only listed if they are compliant with those requirements. Legal requirements: Articles 53(1)(a), 62(1), 63(1) and 64(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3, 4, 6 and 8 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. Recommendation based on conclusion No. 56 Associated findings No. 51, 52, 53 and 54 15

citations.text: In the case of the inspection centre Samskip A/S at the port BCP Aarhus, the audit team noted a number of significant shortcomings with respect to the minimum requirements laid down in Article 64(3) of the OCR and Articles 3 and 4 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014, in particular: · the unloading area was not covered by a roof; · there was no dedicated storage area or room; · the inspection room was not fitted with walls, floors and ceilings that are easy to clean and disinfect, adequate drainage nor adequate natural or artificial light; · the inspection room was also not equipped with a table with smooth washable sur- face easy to clean and disinfect.

The audit team noted that the inspection centre had been subject of an annual check by the Food Inspection Unit prior to the amendment of the checklist, which had identified similar shortcomings concerning the inspection room. Corrective action had been re- quired and implemented by the inspection centre, but as noted above, had not ensured compliance with the minimum requirements. In response to the audit findings, the DVFA withdrew the listing of the inspection centre shortly after completion of the audit.

The audit team visited two control points designated by the competent authority for the performance of identity and physical checks on consignments of non-animal origin and noted that neither control points were compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs, which is not in line with Articles 53(1)(a) of the OCR. In particular: · at one control point, part of the storage area is also used for the inspection of goods and did not have a supply of hot and cold running water and facilities for washing and drying hands which is not in line with Article 3(1)(b) of Implementing Regula- tion (EU) 2019/1014. Neither did it have a table for performing inspections (these 13 were carried out on a pile of wooden pallets), nor cleaning and disinfection equip- ment. · at the second control point, the audit team noted that the designated storage area was not adequate for the number of consignments received, and that consignments were stored outside of the designated storage area. The inspection room itself is also used for other activities, including the storing of administrative documents, and was not easy to disinfect or clean, which is not in line with Articles 3(2) and 4(1) of Imple- menting Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team noted that the DVFA checks were carried out prior to the amendment of the checklists and had not therefore identified the above issues. Conclusions on the compliance of border control posts with minimum requirements

Despite those measures, the audit identified shortcomings in one inspection centre at one BCP, and at both control points evaluated. The competent authority has strengthened their verification checks and took action during the audit to delist the non-compliant inspection centre. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The audit found that there is a system of official controls in place for animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Denmark, which is supported by suitably qualified and experienced staff, and cooperation and communication within and between the competent authorities. The official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs are generally carried out in line with relevant EU legislation. However, shortcomings were identified in the documented procedures for the performance of official controls on animals and goods of non-animal origin, the decision making and follow- up of non-compliant consignments of animals and goods, and the compliance of control points with minimum requirements, which undermine the overall effectiveness of the official controls and their compliance with EU legislation. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 15 November 2024 with representatives of the competent au- thorities during which, the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were pre- sented by the audit team. 14 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authority is invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, includ- ing deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below. With regards to the non-compliances noted in the audit report which did not result in a recommendation being made, the competent authority is, nevertheless, invited to address those. The effectiveness of the actions taken to address such non-compliances will be assessed in future audits on this topic. audits.title: evaluate controls on residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants in animals and animal products

recommendations.text: To ensure that for the national risk-based control plan for residues of pharmacologically active substances, all sampling in slaughterhouses is targeted. Legal basis: Points 3 and 4 of Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2022/1644. Recommendation based on conclusion 32. Associated finding 4.
recommendations.legal_basis: Points 3 and 4 of Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2022/1644. Recommendation based on conclusion 32. Associated finding 4.

citations.text: BACKGROUND 4.1. Legal framework for controls on residues in animals and food of animal origin Member States are legally obliged to implement control plans for residues of pharmacologically active substances in animals and animal products (2). These comprise three plans: a national risk-based control plan for production in the Member States, a national randomised surveillance plan for production in the Member States and a national risk-based control plan for third-country imports into the EU. The plans are subject to annual Commission evaluation (3). Member States must establish multiannual national control programmes for pesticides residues (4) in food and feed of both animal and non-animal origin and they must also participate in the multiannual Union control programme (5). Member States must control the presence of certain contaminants in food of both animal and non-animal origin. The foodstuffs of animal origin to be tested and the categories of contaminants to be tested are specified (6) as is the sampling frequency (7). This control plan is also subject to annual Commission evaluation (8). The scope of this report is limited to the competent authorities' implementation of control plans for residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants in animals and animal products. It does not cover the controls on residues in food and feed of non-animal origin. 4.2. Previous Commission audits The Commission services last audited the implementation of official controls on residues and contaminants in animals and food of animal origin in Denmark in 2019 (DG(SANTE) 2019-6650 (9). The report of that audit made four recommendations, which were satisfactorily addressed and subsequently closed due to action(s) taken. The control and surveillance plans for residues of pharmacologically active sub- stances, pesticides and contaminants are generally implemented in line with planned arrangements, EU legal requirements and are effective, underpinning assurances on the residues status of food of animal origin. Notwithstanding this positive assess- ment, the practice of randomly sampling animals in slaughterhouses for the risk- based national control plan for residues of pharmacologically active substances, un- dermines the effectiveness of this particular control programme. 5.6. Laboratories, methods of analysis, method validation and internal quality control

The audit team noted that, while no formal designation was needed for the DVFA laboratory, and a co-operation agreement was in place between the DVFA and the (national) subcontracted laboratory, the co-operation agreement was made between the (national) subcontracted laboratory and the foreign sub-contracted laboratory, and thus the foreign laboratory was not appropriately designated, which is not in line with pertinent EU requirements (48).

The DVFA did not audit both national laboratories since they were subject to audits by the Danish national accreditation body every 15 months, which is in line with EU legislation49. The arrangements in place do not ensure adequate co-ordination and collaboration with the foreign laboratory, as there is no direct relationship between the competent authority and the foreign laboratory since the co-operation agreement is not directly between them, which is not in line with EU legislation (50).

OVERALL CONCLUSION The implementation of the control and surveillance plans for residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants is in line with planned arrangements, EU legal requirements and is generally effective, underpinning assurances on the residues status of food of animal origin. All of the laboratories testing samples for residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants taken under the various control and surveillance plans are accredited to EN/ISO/IEC 17025, operate appropriately validated methods and have well-functioning quality control systems in place. For the most part the actions taken in case of non- compliant results are effective and underpin assurances on the chemical safety of food of animal origin. Notwithstanding this positive assessment, three factors weaken the effectiveness of the overall control system. audits.title: Evaluatio of the implementation of prevention and control measures for highly pathogenic avian influenza

recommendations.text: To ensure that poultry establishments apply effective biosecurity measures appropriate to the specific risks present in their location. This includes ensuring that farmers implement measures to prevent the introduction and spread of HPAI, and that official controls verify their application, detect shortcomings, and enforce corrective actions. Articles 10 to 13 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 - on responsibilities on disease prevention and biosecurity. Articles 1(2)(d), 5(2), 138 to 140 and Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 - on general obligations of the competent authorities to have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness of official controls. Recommendation based on main conclusions No 48 and 49, and associated findings No 15 to 19, 66 and 89 to 91.

To ensure that epidemiological enquiries are complete, and that epidemiological links are appropriately investigated and documented. Article 57(2)(c) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 17 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Recommendation based on main conclusion No 93, associated findings No 66, 67, 68 and 69.

citations.text: Official veterinarians use a standard template to carry out the epidemiological enquiries of outbreaks. The template follows the requirements of Article 57 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Most outbreak investigations concluded that wild birds were the source of infection. However, they did not consistently include detail on possible biosecurity breaches. For instance, in one case, minks that had got into the hen house had killed laying hens, but this was not further examined or linked to biosecurity breaches.

The DVFA did not document the tracing back and forward of all possible sources (people, vehicles or otherwise) that may have led to the introduction of the virus to the outbreak or to other possible epidemiological links of the outbreaks. The DVFA acknowledged the lack of records and expressed that there are plans to develop a system to record the steps and conclusions of the investigations of all possible epidemiological links to the cases. This was not in line with Article 57(2) and Article 62 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. 13

In one outbreak, a private veterinarian, not delegated to take official samples, took swabs under the active surveillance program. These tested positive to H5N1. On the day the authorities got the notification from the laboratory, an official veterinarian took official samples, which tested negative. As this was a flock of ducks, where symptoms of H5N1 are usually limited or absent, the competent authority confirmed the outbreak based on the positive laboratory results of the samples taken by the private veterinarian. However, the authorities did not investigate further. They did not trace the private veterinarian's movements, check for cross contamination or carry out serological testing. This was not in line with Article 62 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 17 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The DK-VET carried out epidemiological analysis for each outbreak and each epidemic year. They include findings from the epidemiological investigations and laboratory results, including whole genome sequencing. These reports include information gathered on the outbreaks from the DVFA officials and explore links between viruses detected in poultry and wild birds.

recommendations.text: To establish mechanisms ensuring that official controls tasks and other official activities are delegated to bodies or natural persons who have the equipment, qualifications and expertise as well as freedom of conflict of interest. To ensure that these delegations are described in writing and that the competent authority organize audits or inspections of such bodies or persons Articles 28, 30 to 33 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on main conclusion No 94, associated findings No 31, 68 and 91.

citations.text: Private veterinarians take samples for active and sometimes also for passive surveillance. The DVFA has not delegated official activities, such as sampling within this active surveillance program, to private veterinarians (see also finding 66). This is not in line with Articles 28, 30 and 31 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

In one outbreak, a private veterinarian, not delegated to take official samples, took swabs under the active surveillance program. These tested positive to H5N1. On the day the authorities got the notification from the laboratory, an official veterinarian took official samples, which tested negative. As this was a flock of ducks, where symptoms of H5N1 are usually limited or absent, the competent authority confirmed the outbreak based on the positive laboratory results of the samples taken by the private veterinarian. However, the authorities did not investigate further. They did not trace the private veterinarian's movements, check for cross contamination or carry out serological testing. This was not in line with Article 62 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 17 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The DVFA consistently documented certain verification steps, such as movement derogation reviews and disinfection validations. At the time of the audit, the authorities did not have plans to establish regular biosecurity controls, enforce these proportionally, or delegate and supervise private veterinarians tasked with carrying out official activities. 16 4.2.2 Conclusions on control and eradication
